sections.title: Amazon Bedrock — platform & inference
sections.summary: Fully managed, serverless API access to foundation models from many providers.

items.name: What Amazon Bedrock is
items.summary: Serverless service to build generative AI apps with FMs from multiple providers through one API.
items.details: Bedrock hosts foundation models from Amazon and third-party providers. You call them through an API without provisioning servers or GPUs, and add features such as knowledge bases, agents, guardrails, and evaluation around them.
items.example: A startup adds a chat assistant to its app in two weeks by calling a model on Bedrock instead of hosting one.
items.tip: "Access FMs from several providers with the LEAST operational overhead" → Bedrock. "Full control of instances, training code, or containers" → SageMaker AI.

items.name: Model catalog & providers
items.summary: Choose among text, image, embedding, and multimodal FMs from Amazon and third-party providers.
items.details: Models differ in modality, context length, languages, speed, price, Regions, and customization support. You can swap models without changing infrastructure.
items.example: A team compares a small, fast model and a larger model on the same prompts before choosing one for production.
items.tip: Model selection is driven by your requirements (modality, latency, cost, Region, customization), not by the biggest benchmark score.

items.name: Playgrounds
items.summary: Console chat, text, and image playgrounds for trying models and inference settings without code.
items.details: Playgrounds let you send prompts, adjust parameters such as temperature and maximum tokens, and compare model responses side by side.
items.example: A product manager tests how two models summarize a policy before engineers write any code.
items.tip: Playgrounds are for trying models and settings; production apps call the API.

items.name: Converse API
items.summary: One consistent request format for chatting with different models, including tool use.
items.details: The Converse API standardizes messages, system prompts, inference settings, and tool (function) calling across supported models, so switching models needs minimal code changes.
items.example: A developer switches the app from one provider's model to another by changing only the model ID.
items.tip: "Switch models with minimal code changes" or "one API for chat and tool use" → Converse API.

items.name: On-demand inference
items.summary: Pay per input and output token with no commitment — the default way to call a model.
items.details: On-demand pricing charges for input tokens and output tokens at model-specific rates. It suits variable or unpredictable traffic.
items.example: An internal assistant with a few hundred requests a day runs on-demand and costs only what it uses.
items.tip: Output tokens usually cost more than input tokens. Long prompts AND long answers both drive cost.

items.name: Batch inference
items.summary: Process large sets of prompts asynchronously from Amazon S3 at a lower price than on-demand.
items.details: You upload JSONL prompts to S3, submit a batch job, and collect outputs in S3. Supported models are priced at a discount to on-demand. Results are not immediate.
items.example: A publisher summarizes 3 million archived articles over a weekend.
items.tip: "Large volume, no user waiting, MOST cost-effective" → batch inference, not Provisioned Throughput.

items.name: Provisioned Throughput
items.summary: Buy dedicated model units for guaranteed throughput, billed hourly, optionally with a commitment.
items.details: Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity for a model. It suits steady, high-volume production traffic and can be used for customized models.
items.example: A customer-facing app with heavy, steady traffic around the clock buys model units for predictable performance.
items.tip: Needs steady volume to pay off. Spiky or low traffic → on-demand (plus cross-Region inference for bursts).

items.name: Cross-Region inference
items.summary: Inference profiles that route on-demand requests across several Regions to absorb traffic bursts.
items.details: Geographic profiles (for example US or EU) keep processing inside one geography. Global profiles can route to any supported commercial Region.
items.example: An EU company uses an EU inference profile to avoid throttling while keeping processing inside the EU.
items.tip: Data residency requirement → geographic profile, not global.

items.name: Service tiers
items.summary: Choose Priority, Standard, or Flex processing per request to trade price against response speed.
items.details: Priority costs more for the fastest responses, Standard is the default, and Flex is discounted for work that can wait. Reserved capacity is arranged separately.
items.example: Nightly evaluation jobs use the Flex tier; the customer chat uses Priority during peak hours.
items.tip: Fastest responses, pay more → Priority. Work that can wait, pay less → Flex. Guaranteed capacity → reservation.

items.name: Intelligent Prompt Routing
items.summary: Automatically sends each request to a smaller or larger model in the same family to cut cost.
items.details: A prompt router predicts response quality for each request and picks the most cost-effective model that can handle it.
items.example: Simple FAQ questions go to a small model; complex analysis goes to a larger one, automatically.
items.tip: Routing chooses between models per request. Distillation creates a new smaller model. Cross-Region inference spreads load across Regions.

items.name: Prompt caching
items.summary: Reuse a repeated prompt prefix to lower input cost and latency on supported models.
items.details: When many requests share a long prefix (system prompt, documents, examples), the cached portion is not fully reprocessed, and cached tokens are billed at a lower rate.
items.example: A chatbot sends the same 6,000-token policy prompt with every question; caching cuts cost and time to first token.
items.tip: "Same long prefix on every request" + reduce cost AND latency → prompt caching.

items.name: Model invocation logging
items.summary: Record full prompts and responses to Amazon S3 or CloudWatch Logs for audit and analysis.
items.details: Invocation logging is off by default. When enabled, it captures request and response data, so protect the logs with access controls, encryption, and retention.
items.example: A regulated bank keeps every prompt and response for its auditors.
items.tip: CloudTrail records WHO called the API and WHEN — not the prompt text. Full content → invocation logging.

items.name: Data privacy & security
items.summary: Your prompts and outputs aren't used to train base models or shared with model providers.
items.details: Data is encrypted in transit and at rest. You can add customer managed KMS keys, IAM policies that restrict models, and private connectivity with AWS PrivateLink.
items.example: A security team approves Bedrock because customer data never reaches model providers.
items.tip: Bedrock doesn't use your prompts to train base models or share them with providers — a frequent correct answer.

items.name: Amazon Bedrock Marketplace
items.summary: Discover and deploy additional specialized models onto managed endpoints for use with Bedrock APIs.
items.details: Marketplace models run on endpoints that you size and pay for, while still being usable with Bedrock tools such as agents and guardrails.
items.example: A company deploys a niche domain model from the marketplace alongside the serverless models it already uses.
items.tip: Marketplace models run on endpoints you size and pay for, unlike serverless on-demand models.

items.name: Monitoring with CloudWatch
items.summary: Track invocations, latency, token counts, errors, and throttles as Amazon CloudWatch metrics.
items.details: Bedrock publishes runtime metrics that you can chart and alarm on, which helps with cost control and capacity planning.
items.example: An alarm fires when throttled requests spike, prompting the team to add a cross-Region inference profile.
items.tip: Invocation counts, latency, tokens → CloudWatch metrics. Who called → CloudTrail. Prompt text → invocation logging.

sections.title: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
sections.summary: Fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG): ingest, chunk, embed, store, retrieve, cite.

items.name: What Knowledge Bases do
items.summary: Connect FMs to your own data so that answers are grounded in current documents with citations.
items.details: A knowledge base ingests documents from data sources, splits them into chunks, converts them to embeddings, stores them in a vector store, and retrieves relevant chunks at query time.
items.example: An HR assistant answers policy questions from 50,000 PDFs in S3 and links to the source page.
items.tip: "Company data that changes often" + "cite sources" + "least operational overhead" → Knowledge Bases, not fine-tuning.

items.name: Data sources
items.summary: Ingest from Amazon S3, web crawlers, Confluence, SharePoint, Salesforce, and custom sources.
items.details: Connectors pull documents into the knowledge base. A sync (ingestion job) updates the index when source content changes.
items.example: The team re-syncs the knowledge base after legal updates the policy folder in S3.
items.tip: New documents don't appear until the data source is synced (ingested) again.

items.name: Parsing options
items.summary: Default text parsing, or FM-based parsing for tables, figures, and complex layouts.
items.details: Advanced parsing uses a foundation model to interpret visually rich documents so that tables and charts are captured correctly.
items.example: Engineering manuals full of tables are parsed with an FM so that specifications are retrieved accurately.
items.tip: Tables and charts extracted poorly → use FM-based (advanced) parsing.

items.name: Chunking strategies
items.summary: Fixed-size, hierarchical, semantic, no chunking, or custom chunking through AWS Lambda.
items.details: Chunk size trades precision for context. Hierarchical chunking retrieves small child chunks but returns their larger parent context; semantic chunking splits on meaning.
items.example: Answers were missing steps because procedures were split mid-way, so the team switched to hierarchical chunking.
items.tip: Chunks too small → missing context; too large → diluted relevance and more tokens.

items.name: Embeddings model
items.summary: Converts each chunk and each query into a vector, for example Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2.
items.details: The same embeddings model must be used for documents and queries. Vector dimensions must match the vector store index.
items.example: The team picks a multilingual embeddings model because documents are in English and Spanish.
items.tip: Embeddings model → vectors. Text generation model → the final answer. Reranker → reorders results.

items.name: Vector store options
items.summary: OpenSearch Serverless/managed, Aurora PostgreSQL, Neptune Analytics, S3 Vectors, and third-party stores.
items.details: Bedrock can quick-create a vector store for you or connect to one you manage. Third-party options include Pinecone, Redis Enterprise Cloud, and MongoDB Atlas.
items.example: A team already running Aurora PostgreSQL stores its embeddings there with pgvector.
items.tip: Quick-create options remove setup work; bring your own store when you already run one.

items.name: Retrieve vs RetrieveAndGenerate
items.summary: Retrieve returns relevant chunks only; RetrieveAndGenerate also writes an answer with citations.
items.details: Use Retrieve when your application wants to build its own prompt; use RetrieveAndGenerate for a managed end-to-end RAG response.
items.example: A custom agent calls Retrieve and combines the chunks with CRM data in its own prompt.
items.tip: Want chunks for your own prompt → Retrieve. Want a managed answer with citations → RetrieveAndGenerate.

items.name: Metadata filtering
items.summary: Restrict retrieval to documents whose attributes match, such as product version or department.
items.details: You attach metadata to source documents and apply filters at query time. This removes semantically similar but wrong documents.
items.example: Customers with the newest product only receive instructions from the newest manual.
items.tip: Similar documents but wrong version/department/Region returned → metadata filtering.

items.name: Reranking
items.summary: A reranker model re-scores retrieved chunks so that the most relevant ones reach the prompt.
items.details: Reranking improves precision after the initial vector search, often allowing fewer, better chunks to be sent to the model.
items.example: Retrieval returns 20 chunks; a reranker keeps the best 5.
items.tip: Improve relevance of retrieved chunks after vector search → reranker model.

items.name: Hybrid search
items.summary: Combines semantic (vector) search with keyword search for better recall on exact terms.
items.details: Hybrid search helps when queries include product codes, names, or rare terms that pure semantic search can miss. It needs a vector store that supports it.
items.example: Searching for part number "X-4471" works because keyword matching is combined with semantic search.
items.tip: Exact codes or rare terms missed by semantic search → hybrid (keyword + vector) search.

items.name: Source attribution (citations)
items.summary: Responses can include references to the retrieved passages used to answer.
items.details: Citations let users verify answers and reduce the impact of hallucinations.
items.example: Each chatbot answer links to the exact paragraph of the HR policy it used.
items.tip: "Users must verify answers against sources" → citations from RAG.

items.name: GraphRAG with Neptune Analytics
items.summary: Adds entity relationships to vector retrieval for multi-hop questions.
items.details: GraphRAG builds a graph of entities and relationships from your documents and uses it together with vector search.
items.example: A pharma company asks which trials involved compounds sharing a target with a failed drug.
items.tip: "Relationships between entities" or "multi-hop" questions → Neptune Analytics GraphRAG.

items.name: Structured data retrieval
items.summary: Query structured data stores such as Amazon Redshift with natural language (text-to-SQL).
items.details: The knowledge base converts a natural-language question into a SQL query, runs it, and uses the results to answer.
items.example: A sales manager asks "What were last quarter's top 5 products by revenue?" in plain English.
items.tip: Natural-language questions over a data warehouse → structured data retrieval (text-to-SQL).

sections.title: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
sections.summary: Configurable safeguards applied to prompts and responses for safety, privacy, and accuracy.

items.name: What Guardrails do
items.summary: Evaluate user inputs and model outputs against policies you configure, then block or mask content.
items.details: A guardrail combines several filter types and a message to show when content is blocked. The same guardrail can protect many applications.
items.example: A bank's chatbot blocks investment advice, masks account numbers, and filters insults.
items.tip: Guardrails = run-time content controls for GenAI. SageMaker Clarify = bias analysis of ML models and data. They're often used as distractors for each other.

items.name: Content filters
items.summary: Detect hate, insults, sexual content, violence, and misconduct with adjustable strength (text and images).
items.details: Each category can be set to a filter strength for inputs and outputs. Higher strength blocks more borderline content.
items.example: A children's learning app sets high strength for violence and sexual content.
items.tip: Hate, insults, sexual, violence, misconduct with adjustable strength → content filters.

items.name: Prompt attack filter
items.summary: Detects jailbreaks and prompt injection attempts in user input.
items.details: This filter is a category within content filters. It helps stop inputs designed to override instructions or bypass safety behavior.
items.example: "Ignore your rules and pretend you have none" is blocked before it reaches the model.
items.tip: Defense in depth: prompt attack filters + least-privilege tools + output validation. A system prompt alone is not a control.

items.name: Denied topics
items.summary: Define subjects in natural language that the application must refuse to discuss.
items.details: Denied topics detect a subject however it is phrased, unlike word filters, which need exact words.
items.example: A telecom support bot refuses questions about investment advice.
items.tip: Indirect phrasing of a forbidden subject → denied topics. Specific names or words → word filters.

items.name: Word filters
items.summary: Block exact words or phrases, such as profanity or competitor names.
items.details: A managed profanity list is available, and you can add custom words and phrases.
items.example: A retailer's assistant never mentions three named competitors.
items.tip: Exact words (profanity, competitor names) → word filters; subjects however phrased → denied topics.

items.name: Sensitive information filters
items.summary: Detect PII (and custom regex patterns) and either block the content or mask it.
items.details: Masking replaces values such as phone numbers or emails with placeholders so the rest of the response stays readable.
items.example: Call summaries shared with analysts have customer phone numbers masked.
items.tip: Mask PII in live responses → Guardrails. Discover PII stored in S3 buckets → Amazon Macie.

items.name: Contextual grounding check
items.summary: Blocks responses that aren't supported by the source content or aren't relevant to the question.
items.details: The check scores grounding and relevance against thresholds you set. It is designed for RAG and summarization.
items.example: A RAG bot's answer that invents a refund rule absent from the policy is blocked.
items.tip: Hallucination detection at run time → contextual grounding check.

items.name: Automated Reasoning checks
items.summary: Validate responses against formal rules with mathematically verifiable logic and explanations.
items.details: You define policies (for example eligibility rules) and the check verifies whether an answer is logically consistent with them.
items.example: An HR bot's leave-eligibility answers are verified against precise service-length and hours rules.
items.tip: Precise, rule-based correctness → Automated Reasoning. Faithfulness to retrieved passages → contextual grounding.

items.name: ApplyGuardrail API
items.summary: Use a guardrail on any text, including for models hosted outside Amazon Bedrock.
items.details: The API evaluates input or output text against a guardrail without invoking a Bedrock model.
items.example: One guardrail protects both a Bedrock app and a self-hosted model on SageMaker AI.
items.tip: "Same policies for Bedrock and non-Bedrock models" → ApplyGuardrail API.

sections.title: Amazon Bedrock Agents & Flows
sections.summary: Managed agents that plan multi-step tasks and call APIs, plus visual generative AI workflows.

items.name: Amazon Bedrock Agents
items.summary: An FM that reasons through a task, calls APIs, and queries knowledge bases to complete it.
items.details: The agent breaks down the user's request, decides which action to take, calls tools, and uses the results until the task is done.
items.example: A travel agent looks up a booking, checks the change policy, and rebooks the flight.
items.tip: Agents can ACT (call APIs). A knowledge base alone can only retrieve.

items.name: Action groups
items.summary: Define the APIs an agent can call, with an OpenAPI schema or function definitions, usually backed by Lambda.
items.details: Each action group describes available operations and their parameters so the agent knows when and how to call them.
items.example: A "Reservations" action group exposes search, book, and cancel operations.
items.tip: How an agent calls your API → action group with an OpenAPI schema (or function details) + Lambda.

items.name: Knowledge base association
items.summary: Attach knowledge bases so the agent can retrieve information while completing tasks.
items.details: The agent decides when to query a knowledge base, for example to check a policy before taking an action.
items.example: A claims agent checks the coverage policy before approving a claim.
items.tip: Agent needs policy facts before acting → attach a knowledge base.

items.name: User confirmation & return of control
items.summary: Require the user to confirm before an action runs, or return control to the app to execute it.
items.details: These are enforced by the agent's orchestration, not by prompt instructions, which makes them reliable for high-impact actions.
items.example: A refund is only issued after the customer confirms the amount.
items.tip: Human-in-the-loop for risky actions must be enforced by orchestration, not by a system prompt instruction.

items.name: Agent memory
items.summary: Retain summaries of past sessions so an agent can continue across conversations.
items.details: Memory lets the agent remember context from earlier sessions for the same user, within limits you configure.
items.example: A support agent remembers the customer's open case from yesterday's chat.
items.tip: Remember context across sessions for the same user → agent memory.

items.name: Multi-agent collaboration
items.summary: A supervisor agent coordinates specialist agents to solve complex tasks.
items.details: Each specialist handles a focused responsibility; the supervisor delegates and combines results.
items.example: A financial-report agent delegates data gathering and analysis to two specialist agents.
items.tip: Complex task split among specialists with a coordinator → multi-agent collaboration (supervisor).

items.name: Amazon Bedrock Flows
items.summary: Visually link prompts, models, knowledge bases, Lambda functions, and conditions into a workflow.
items.details: Flows orchestrate fixed, repeatable generative AI pipelines, which suits predictable processes better than an autonomous agent.
items.example: A document pipeline extracts fields, summarizes, and routes exceptions — always in the same order.
items.tip: Fixed steps + auditability → workflow (Flows). Unknown path, tool choice at run time → agent.

sections.title: Amazon Bedrock model customization
sections.summary: Adapt foundation models with your own data: fine-tuning, reinforcement fine-tuning, distillation, import.

items.name: Supervised fine-tuning
items.summary: Train a copy of a model on labeled prompt-response examples to change its behavior or style.
items.details: Fine-tuning adjusts model weights using your examples. It needs a quality labeled dataset and creates a private custom model.
items.example: A bank fine-tunes on 20,000 approved letters so outputs follow its house style.
items.tip: Consistent style or behavior → fine-tuning. Facts that change often → RAG.

items.name: Reinforcement fine-tuning
items.summary: Improve a model with feedback from reward functions instead of labeled answers.
items.details: You provide prompts and reward logic (for example in AWS Lambda) that scores responses; the model learns to maximize the reward.
items.example: A code assistant is rewarded when generated code passes unit tests.
items.tip: No labeled answers but a way to score responses → reinforcement fine-tuning.

items.name: Model distillation
items.summary: Transfer a large teacher model's quality to a smaller, faster, cheaper student model.
items.details: Bedrock generates teacher responses from your prompts and fine-tunes the student on them.
items.example: A claims-triage task keeps near-teacher accuracy at a fraction of the cost.
items.tip: "Large model is accurate but too slow/expensive" → distillation.

items.name: Custom Model Import
items.summary: Bring model weights you customized elsewhere into Bedrock and invoke them serverlessly.
items.details: Supported open model architectures trained or fine-tuned outside Bedrock (for example in SageMaker AI) can be imported and used through Bedrock APIs.
items.example: A team fine-tunes an open-weight model in SageMaker AI, then imports it to Bedrock for serverless inference.
items.tip: Weights customized outside Bedrock + want serverless inference → Custom Model Import.

items.name: Training data format
items.summary: Labeled examples in JSON Lines (JSONL) files stored in Amazon S3, with an optional validation set.
items.details: Each record contains a prompt and its desired response (or a conversation). Quality, consistency, and representativeness matter more than volume.
items.example: The team uploads train.jsonl and validation.jsonl to S3 before starting the job.
items.tip: Instruction-based fine-tuning data = prompt-response pairs.

items.name: Custom model costs
items.summary: Training (tokens × epochs) + monthly model storage + inference (on-demand or Provisioned Throughput).
items.details: Customization adds upfront and ongoing costs compared with prompting or RAG, and it must be repeated to add new knowledge.
items.example: The budget includes the training job, monthly storage, and inference for the custom model.
items.tip: Custom models add training + storage + inference costs, and must be retrained to add knowledge.

sections.title: Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management
sections.summary: Create, version, test, and share prompts separately from application code.

items.name: Prompt templates & variables
items.summary: Reusable prompts with placeholders that are filled in at run time.
items.details: Templates standardize instructions and output format while the variable input changes.
items.example: Every transcript summary uses the same template with a {{transcript}} variable.
items.tip: Consistent outputs across many users with the least effort → prompt template.

items.name: Prompt versions
items.summary: Immutable snapshots of a prompt that applications reference for safe rollout and rollback.
items.details: Applications can point to a specific version, so reverting a bad change doesn't need a code deployment.
items.example: After quality drops, the app switches back to version 3 immediately.
items.tip: Auditable prompt history + quick rollback → Prompt Management versions.

items.name: Variants & comparison
items.summary: Compare prompt variants and models side by side on the same inputs.
items.details: Experimentation with variants helps pick the best prompt with evidence rather than intuition.
items.example: Two wording variants are compared on the same 50 claims before release.
items.tip: Choose between prompts with evidence → compare variants on the same representative inputs.

items.name: Prompt optimization
items.summary: Automatically rewrites a prompt to follow best practices for a chosen model.
items.details: Optimization is a starting point that you still evaluate on representative data.
items.example: A developer optimizes a draft prompt for a new model before testing it.
items.tip: Prompt optimization gives a better starting prompt — you still evaluate it.

sections.title: Amazon Bedrock Evaluations
sections.summary: Evaluate and compare models and RAG sources with automatic, judge-model, or human evaluation.

items.name: Automatic (programmatic) evaluation
items.summary: Compute metrics such as accuracy, robustness, and toxicity on built-in or custom datasets.
items.details: A quick, low-effort baseline for comparing candidate models before building your own test set.
items.example: A team compares three models on summarization accuracy and toxicity in an afternoon.
items.tip: Quick, low-effort model comparison on accuracy, robustness, toxicity → automatic evaluation.

items.name: LLM-as-a-judge
items.summary: A second model scores responses against criteria such as correctness, helpfulness, and harmfulness.
items.details: Scales rubric-based evaluation to thousands of responses without reference answers. Calibrate it with periodic human review.
items.example: 20,000 weekly chatbot answers are scored for helpfulness and tone.
items.tip: No reference answers + large volume + subjective criteria → LLM-as-a-judge.

items.name: Human-based evaluation
items.summary: Your own reviewers rate or compare responses against criteria you define.
items.details: Best for subjective, expert, or brand-specific quality that automatic metrics can't capture.
items.example: A luxury brand's copy editors judge whether descriptions match the brand voice.
items.tip: Subjective or expert judgment (brand voice, empathy) → human-based evaluation.

items.name: RAG (knowledge base) evaluation
items.summary: Measure retrieval quality (context relevance, coverage) and generation quality (faithfulness, correctness).
items.details: Separating retrieval metrics from generation metrics shows which stage causes wrong answers.
items.example: The right passages were retrieved but the answer added a condition → low faithfulness → a generation problem.
items.tip: Wrong or missing context → retrieval issue. Right context, wrong answer → generation issue.

sections.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
sections.summary: Services to deploy, connect, secure, and operate AI agents built with any framework or model.

items.name: What AgentCore is
items.summary: Modular infrastructure for production agents — use the pieces you need, with any framework.
items.details: AgentCore works with frameworks such as Strands Agents, LangGraph, or CrewAI and with models inside or outside Bedrock.
items.example: A team moves its LangGraph prototype to production without rewriting it.
items.tip: Bedrock Agents = fully managed agent builder. AgentCore = building blocks to run your own agent code.

items.name: AgentCore Runtime
items.summary: Serverless hosting for agents and tools with session isolation and support for long-running tasks.
items.details: Each session runs isolated, scales automatically, and supports multi-step work that takes a long time.
items.example: Several agents built with different frameworks are hosted without managing servers.
items.tip: Host agents from any framework, serverless, isolated sessions, long-running → AgentCore Runtime (not Lambda).

items.name: AgentCore Memory
items.summary: Short-term memory for the current session and long-term memory for facts and preferences across sessions.
items.details: Long-term memory extracts durable information, such as user preferences or summaries, so it can be recalled later.
items.example: A travel agent remembers a traveler's seat preference weeks later.
items.tip: Remember across sessions → long-term memory — not a bigger context window, not fine-tuning.

items.name: AgentCore Gateway
items.summary: Turns existing APIs, Lambda functions, and services into MCP-compatible tools for agents.
items.details: Agents can discover and call tools through one endpoint without each API being rewritten as an MCP server.
items.example: Dozens of internal REST APIs become tools that any company agent can use.
items.tip: "Expose existing APIs to agents via MCP" → Gateway.

items.name: AgentCore Identity
items.summary: Manages agent identities and credentials so agents can act on behalf of users (for example with OAuth).
items.details: It handles inbound authorization and outbound access to AWS and third-party services with a secure token vault.
items.example: An agent updates a third-party CRM using each employee's own OAuth permissions.
items.tip: Agent needs user-delegated access to other systems → AgentCore Identity (not shared keys, not Memory).

items.name: Policy in AgentCore
items.summary: Deterministic rules (Cedar) that allow or block agent tool calls at the Gateway.
items.details: Policies check who the user is and the tool's parameters before the call runs, outside the agent's code and prompt.
items.example: Refunds over $500, or for another customer's account, are always blocked.
items.tip: Deterministic limits on agent actions → Policy in AgentCore. Guardrails filter content, not tool authorization.

items.name: AgentCore Observability
items.summary: Traces, metrics, and logs of agent steps, tool calls, and model calls, viewable in CloudWatch.
items.details: Observability shows each step an agent took, which helps debugging, auditing, and performance tuning.
items.example: The team traces why an agent called the wrong tool on step 3.
items.tip: Observability detects and explains; it doesn't prevent actions (that's Policy).

items.name: AgentCore Code Interpreter
items.summary: A secure sandbox where agents write and run code for exact calculations and data analysis.
items.details: LLMs predict tokens and make arithmetic mistakes; running code gives exact results.
items.example: A finance assistant computes statistics over a 50,000-row spreadsheet exactly.
items.tip: Exact calculations or data analysis inside an agent → code execution tool.

items.name: AgentCore Browser
items.summary: A managed cloud browser that agents use to navigate and interact with websites.
items.details: The browser runs in an isolated environment, so agents can complete web tasks without local infrastructure.
items.example: An agent fills in a supplier's web form that has no API.
items.tip: Agent must use a website that has no API → AgentCore Browser.

items.name: AgentCore Evaluations
items.summary: Evaluate agent quality, such as goal success and correct tool use, on real interactions.
items.details: Agent evaluation looks at outcomes and at the trajectory (tools chosen, parameters, steps), not just final wording.
items.example: A room-booking agent is scored on whether the correct room was booked and tools were used correctly.
items.tip: Evaluate agents on task success and tool use, not just final text.

sections.title: Amazon Nova
sections.summary: Amazon's own family of foundation models on Bedrock for text, multimodal, image, video, and speech.

items.name: Nova understanding models (Micro, Lite, Pro, Premier)
items.summary: Micro is text-only and fastest; Lite and Pro accept text, images, and video; Premier is the most capable.
items.details: Choose the smallest model that meets quality. Larger Nova models can act as teachers for distillation.
items.example: A simple text classifier uses Nova Micro; a document-with-images assistant uses Nova Pro.
items.tip: Image input needed → not Micro (text-only).

items.name: Nova Canvas
items.summary: Generate and edit images from text, including inpainting, outpainting, and background removal.
items.details: Supports negative prompts that describe what should not appear in the image.
items.example: A retailer generates product shots and replaces backgrounds.
items.tip: Generate/edit images → Nova Canvas. Analyze images → Amazon Rekognition.

items.name: Nova Reel
items.summary: Generate short videos from text and image prompts.
items.details: Useful for marketing and creative content that needs motion.
items.example: A travel company creates a short destination clip for social media.
items.tip: Generate video → Nova Reel. Generate images → Nova Canvas.

items.name: Nova Sonic
items.summary: Speech-to-speech model for natural, real-time voice conversations.
items.details: It combines understanding and generation of speech in one model, rather than chaining separate speech-to-text and text-to-speech steps.
items.example: A voice assistant answers phone calls with natural turn-taking.
items.tip: Real-time spoken conversation in one model → Nova Sonic (vs chaining Transcribe + LLM + Polly).

sections.title: Strands Agents
sections.summary: Open-source, model-driven SDK for building AI agents in a few lines of code.

items.name: What Strands Agents is
items.summary: Define a model, a prompt, and tools; the model decides which tools to call.
items.details: Strands supports many model providers, native MCP tools, and multi-agent patterns such as swarm, graph, and workflow. It can run on AWS or elsewhere.
items.example: A developer builds a research agent in Python and later hosts it on AgentCore Runtime.
items.tip: Strands = SDK to WRITE agents. AgentCore = services to RUN them. Kiro = IDE to write code.

sections.title: Kiro
sections.summary: Agentic AI development environment with spec-driven development.

items.name: What Kiro is
items.summary: An IDE that turns prompts into specs (requirements, design, tasks) and then code, docs, and tests.
items.details: Agent hooks run actions automatically on events such as saving a file; steering files hold project conventions.
items.example: A team writes a feature request and Kiro produces a spec and task list before coding.
items.tip: Coding assistance / spec-driven development → Kiro. Migrating legacy apps → AWS Transform.

sections.title: Amazon Quick
sections.summary: Ready-to-use AI workspace for business users: agents, research, automation, and BI dashboards.

items.name: What Amazon Quick is
items.summary: Business users chat with AI agents over connected company data and apps — no app to build.
items.details: Quick evolved from Amazon QuickSight and combines BI, research, workflow automation, and app building.
items.example: Analysts ask questions across documents and dashboards and get cited answers.
items.tip: Ready-made assistant for business users → Quick. Building your own GenAI app → Bedrock.

items.name: Quick Sight
items.summary: Interactive dashboards and business intelligence (formerly Amazon QuickSight).
items.details: Connect data sources, build dashboards, and ask questions about data in natural language.
items.example: A sales team explores revenue by region in a dashboard.
items.tip: Dashboards and BI for business users → Quick Sight (formerly QuickSight).

items.name: Quick Research
items.summary: Deep research across the web and your data, delivered as a cited report.
items.details: Research agents gather and synthesize information into a report with sources.
items.example: A strategy team gets a cited market-landscape report.
items.tip: Cited research report across web and company data, no app to build → Quick Research.

items.name: Quick Flows & Quick Automate
items.summary: Automate repetitive tasks and multi-step business processes with AI agents across apps.
items.details: Flows automate everyday tasks; Automate builds larger process automations with agents making decisions.
items.example: Weekly status updates are compiled and posted automatically.
items.tip: Business users automating routine tasks across apps without code → Quick Flows/Automate.

items.name: Quick Index
items.summary: Connect organizational documents and data so AI answers are grounded in company information.
items.details: Indexing company content lets agents answer with your data rather than general knowledge.
items.example: Employees ask about internal policies and get grounded answers.
items.tip: Ground Quick's answers in company documents → Quick Index.

sections.title: AWS Transform
sections.summary: Agentic AI service for migrating and modernizing legacy workloads.

items.name: What AWS Transform is
items.summary: Specialized agents that assess, plan, and transform code and infrastructure, such as .NET, mainframe, and VMware.
items.details: Transform automates large parts of modernization projects that used to be manual.
items.example: A company ports .NET Framework apps to cross-platform .NET.
items.tip: "Modernize/migrate legacy workloads with agentic AI" → AWS Transform.

sections.title: Amazon Q
sections.summary: Generative AI assistants from AWS for developers and for business users.

items.name: Amazon Q Business
items.summary: A generative AI assistant that answers questions and completes tasks using enterprise data.
items.details: It connects to company data sources and respects existing permissions. It is a ready-made assistant, not a model API.
items.example: Employees ask about benefits and get answers from HR documents they're allowed to see.
items.tip: Q Business does not give you raw FM access — for that, use Bedrock or SageMaker JumpStart.

items.name: Amazon Q Developer
items.summary: A coding and AWS assistant in the IDE, command line, and AWS console.
items.details: It helps generate, explain, and transform code and answers questions about AWS resources.
items.example: A developer asks for a unit test and an explanation of an error in their IDE.
items.tip: Coding assistant in the IDE → Q Developer or Kiro; neither is an FM hosting service.

sections.title: SageMaker AI — build & train
sections.summary: Fully managed platform to prepare data and build, train, and tune your own ML models.

items.name: What SageMaker AI is
items.summary: End-to-end ML platform with full control over data, code, frameworks, and infrastructure.
items.details: SageMaker AI covers the ML lifecycle: data preparation, training, tuning, deployment, monitoring, and governance.
items.example: A data science team trains a custom churn model with its own Python code.
items.tip: Custom models and control → SageMaker AI. Serverless access to existing FMs → Bedrock.

items.name: SageMaker Studio
items.summary: Web-based IDE for ML with notebooks (JupyterLab, Code Editor) and access to SageMaker tools.
items.details: Studio is where practitioners write code, run experiments, and manage models in one interface.
items.example: Data scientists explore data and train models from JupyterLab in Studio.
items.tip: Studio is for practitioners who write code; Canvas is for no-code business users.

items.name: SageMaker Canvas
items.summary: No-code visual interface for business analysts to prepare data, build models, and predict.
items.details: Canvas also includes data preparation (Data Wrangler) and access to ready-to-use models and FMs, all without writing code.
items.example: Marketing analysts predict which customers will respond to a promotion from a CSV.
items.tip: "No ML/coding experience" + "build a predictive model" → Canvas.

items.name: Data Wrangler
items.summary: Visual data preparation with hundreds of built-in transformations and data quality insights.
items.details: It imports, cleans, transforms, and analyzes data, then exports it to training or pipelines.
items.example: A team fixes missing values and encodes categories before training.
items.tip: Visual data prep inside SageMaker → Data Wrangler. Standalone visual prep → Glue DataBrew.

items.name: Feature Store
items.summary: Central repository to store, share, and reuse ML features for training and inference.
items.details: Offline storage serves training; online storage serves low-latency inference, which keeps features consistent.
items.example: Every team uses the same "90-day spend" feature definition.
items.tip: Training/serving feature mismatch → Feature Store.

items.name: SageMaker Ground Truth
items.summary: Build labeled datasets with human workforces (private, vendor, public) and automated labeling.
items.details: Ground Truth also supports human feedback workflows, such as ranking model responses for RLHF.
items.example: 500,000 product images are labeled by employees and a vendor workforce.
items.tip: Label TRAINING data → Ground Truth. Human review of LIVE predictions → Amazon A2I.

items.name: Training jobs
items.summary: Managed training on the instances you choose, including distributed and Spot training.
items.details: You provide the algorithm or container and data in S3; SageMaker provisions compute, trains, and saves the model artifact.
items.example: A team trains an XGBoost model on 50 GB of tabular data.
items.tip: Custom training code and full control of instances → SageMaker AI training jobs.

items.name: Automatic Model Tuning
items.summary: Searches hyperparameter combinations to find the best-performing model.
items.details: Tuning runs many training jobs with different hyperparameters and keeps the best by your objective metric.
items.example: The tuning job finds the learning rate and tree depth that maximize validation F1.
items.tip: Hyperparameters are set before training (learning rate, epochs); parameters/weights are learned.

items.name: Autopilot (AutoML)
items.summary: Automatically explores data, tries algorithms, and builds the best model from tabular data.
items.details: AutoML capabilities are available through SageMaker Canvas.
items.example: A team gets a baseline model for predicting late payments with minimal effort.
items.tip: Automatically build the best tabular model with minimal effort → AutoML (Autopilot/Canvas).

items.name: Experiment tracking (MLflow)
items.summary: Track parameters, metrics, and artifacts of experiments to compare and reproduce runs.
items.details: Managed MLflow in SageMaker AI records what data, code, and settings produced each model.
items.example: The team reproduces last month's best model from its tracked run.
items.tip: Reproduce past experiments → track data, code, parameters, and metrics (MLflow).

items.name: SageMaker Pipelines
items.summary: Automate ML workflows (process, train, evaluate, register, deploy) as repeatable pipelines.
items.details: Pipelines are the MLOps backbone for CI/CD of models, with conditional steps such as "register only if accuracy > X".
items.example: Retraining runs weekly and only registers models that beat the current one.
items.tip: Repeatable, automated ML workflow → Pipelines.

items.name: SageMaker HyperPod
items.summary: Resilient, large-scale clusters for training and fine-tuning foundation models.
items.details: HyperPod handles node failures automatically during long distributed training runs.
items.example: A research lab pre-trains its own model across hundreds of accelerators.
items.tip: Pre-train or fine-tune very large models on resilient clusters → HyperPod.

sections.title: SageMaker AI — deploy (inference options)
sections.summary: Four ways to serve predictions: real-time, serverless, asynchronous, and batch transform.

items.name: Real-time inference
items.summary: Persistent endpoints for interactive, low-latency predictions.
items.details: Best for steady traffic where each request needs an immediate response.
items.example: A fraud score is returned in milliseconds during checkout.
items.tip: Latency order: real-time < asynchronous < batch transform.

items.name: Serverless inference
items.summary: Endpoints that scale with traffic without managing instances; tolerates cold starts.
items.details: You pay for compute used, which suits intermittent traffic with idle periods.
items.example: A small internal classifier used during business hours only.
items.tip: Intermittent traffic + cold starts OK + no instance management → serverless.

items.name: Asynchronous inference
items.summary: Queues requests with large payloads (up to 1 GB) and long processing (up to 1 hour).
items.details: Results go to Amazon S3 with optional notifications, and the endpoint can scale in to zero.
items.example: Uploaded videos are analyzed in 5–20 minutes and users are notified.
items.tip: Large payload / long processing / near-real-time → asynchronous.

items.name: Batch transform
items.summary: Offline predictions for a whole dataset, with no persistent endpoint.
items.details: Compute is provisioned only while the job runs, and results are written to S3.
items.example: A bank scores 12 million loans at month-end.
items.tip: Whole dataset on a schedule → batch transform.

items.name: Multi-model endpoints
items.summary: Host many models behind one endpoint to share infrastructure and lower cost.
items.details: Models are loaded on demand, which suits many similar, infrequently used models.
items.example: A SaaS company serves a separate small model per customer on one endpoint.
items.tip: Many small, rarely used models → multi-model endpoint to save cost.

items.name: Inference Recommender
items.summary: Load-tests a model on different instance types to recommend the best cost/performance.
items.details: It removes guesswork when choosing endpoint instance types.
items.example: A team picks the cheapest instance that meets its 50 ms latency target.
items.tip: Pick the cheapest instance that meets latency → Inference Recommender.

sections.title: SageMaker AI — governance & responsible AI
sections.summary: Tools to detect bias, explain predictions, monitor models, document, and control them.

items.name: Clarify — bias detection
items.summary: Measures bias in training data (pre-training) and in model predictions (post-training).
items.details: Metrics include class imbalance and differences in positive outcomes between groups.
items.example: A lender checks whether applicants over 60 are underrepresented before training.
items.tip: Bias in ML data/predictions → Clarify. Filtering harmful GenAI content → Guardrails.

items.name: Clarify — explainability
items.summary: Feature attributions (SHAP values) that show which inputs drove a prediction.
items.details: Local explanations cover one prediction; global importance summarizes features across all predictions.
items.example: An insurer shows which factors drove one customer's premium.
items.tip: Why did the model predict THIS? → Clarify SHAP (local) explanations.

items.name: Clarify — FM evaluation
items.summary: Evaluate foundation models for accuracy, robustness, toxicity, and stereotyping.
items.details: Useful for comparing FMs on responsible AI dimensions before choosing one.
items.example: A team checks candidate models for stereotyping before launch.
items.tip: Compare FMs for stereotyping or toxicity → Clarify FM evaluation or Bedrock evaluations.

items.name: Model Monitor
items.summary: Continuously checks deployed models for data quality, model quality, bias drift, and attribution drift.
items.details: It compares live traffic against a baseline and raises alerts (CloudWatch) when violations occur.
items.example: An alert fires when a credit model's input distributions shift after a new product launch.
items.tip: Monitoring in production → Model Monitor (uses Clarify for bias drift). Response to drift → retrain.

items.name: Model Registry
items.summary: Catalog of model versions with metrics and an approval status used to gate deployment.
items.details: CI/CD pipelines can deploy only versions that are Approved.
items.example: A manager approves version 12 before it goes to production.
items.tip: Versions + approvals → Registry. Governance documentation → Model Cards.

items.name: Model Cards
items.summary: Single record of a model's intended uses, risk rating, training details, and evaluation results.
items.details: Cards support governance and audits and can be exported.
items.example: A bank's model risk team keeps a card for every credit model.
items.tip: Your models → SageMaker Model Cards. AWS's own AI services → AWS AI Service Cards.

items.name: Model Dashboard
items.summary: Central view of all models, endpoints, and monitoring status in an account.
items.details: It helps governance teams see which models are deployed and whether monitors are alerting.
items.example: A platform lead spots endpoints that have no monitoring schedule.
items.tip: One view of all models and their monitoring status → Model Dashboard.

items.name: Role Manager
items.summary: Quickly create least-privilege IAM roles for ML personas and activities.
items.details: Predefined personas (such as data scientist or MLOps engineer) speed up secure access setup.
items.example: New data scientists get scoped permissions on day one.
items.tip: Quick least-privilege roles for ML personas → Role Manager.

items.name: Amazon Augmented AI (A2I)
items.summary: Human review workflows for ML predictions, for example when confidence is low.
items.details: A2I has built-in integration with Amazon Textract and Amazon Rekognition and can be used with custom models.
items.example: Low-confidence loan document extractions go to a human before use.
items.tip: Human-in-the-loop for LIVE predictions → A2I. Labeling TRAINING data → Ground Truth.

items.name: ML Lineage Tracking
items.summary: Records the data, code, jobs, and models involved in producing each model version.
items.details: Lineage answers audit questions about where a model's training data came from.
items.example: An auditor traces model v7 back to its source datasets and processing jobs.
items.tip: Trace a model back to its data and jobs → lineage tracking.

sections.title: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
sections.summary: ML hub of pre-trained and open-source models (including FMs) that you deploy and fine-tune in your account.

items.name: What JumpStart is
items.summary: Browse, deploy, and fine-tune hundreds of pre-trained models with a few clicks or lines of code.
items.details: Models deploy to SageMaker AI endpoints in your account, where you choose instances and networking.
items.example: A team deploys an open-weight LLM inside its VPC and later fine-tunes it.
items.tip: Open-source FM + control of instances/VPC → JumpStart. Fully serverless FM API → Bedrock.

items.name: Fine-tuning in JumpStart
items.summary: Fine-tune supported models on your data with managed training jobs.
items.details: You bring your dataset in S3 and run a training job; the result is deployed to an endpoint you manage.
items.example: A legal firm fine-tunes an open model on its clause library.
items.tip: Fine-tune an open model you host yourself → JumpStart; serverless customization → Bedrock.

items.name: Model licenses
items.summary: Each model has its own license and terms — review them before commercial use.
items.details: Open-source does not always mean unrestricted use.
items.example: Legal checks a model's license before it's used in a paid product.
items.tip: Transparency and legal risk: check licensing and data provenance of third-party models.

items.name: Private curated hubs
items.summary: Curate an approved subset of models for your organization.
items.details: Administrators control which models teams may discover and deploy.
items.example: Only security-approved models appear in the company's hub.
items.tip: Only approved models available to teams → private curated hub.

sections.title: Amazon Comprehend
sections.summary: Managed NLP: extract sentiment, entities, key phrases, language, and PII from text.

items.name: Sentiment analysis
items.summary: Classify text as positive, negative, neutral, or mixed.
items.details: Works on text you already have; it can't read images or audio.
items.example: Managers find which support tickets express negative sentiment.
items.tip: Audio calls → Transcribe first, then Comprehend.

items.name: Entities & key phrases
items.summary: Find people, places, organizations, dates, products, and key phrases in text.
items.details: Useful for tagging and routing documents automatically.
items.example: Customer reviews are tagged with the products they mention.
items.tip: Find product names or organizations in text → entities (custom entities for your own types).

items.name: Language detection
items.summary: Identify the dominant language of a text.
items.details: Often used before translation or routing.
items.example: Emails are routed to the right regional team by language.
items.tip: Detect the language of text → Comprehend. Detect the spoken language in audio → Transcribe.

items.name: PII detection & redaction
items.summary: Detect and redact personal data in text you send to Comprehend.
items.details: It processes text you provide, unlike Macie, which scans data at rest in S3.
items.example: Support transcripts are redacted before sharing with analysts.
items.tip: PII in text you submit → Comprehend (or Guardrails for GenAI). PII across S3 buckets → Macie.

items.name: Custom classification
items.summary: Train a classifier on your own labeled documents, in multi-class or multi-label mode.
items.details: Custom models learn your own categories with no ML expertise needed.
items.example: Support tickets are routed to Billing, Technical, or Account.
items.tip: Route documents into your own categories without ML expertise → custom classification.

items.name: Custom entity recognition
items.summary: Train Comprehend to find entity types specific to your business.
items.details: Useful for policy numbers, part codes, or product names that general models miss.
items.example: Insurance claims are scanned for policy numbers.
items.tip: Custom entities find terms in text — they don't fix misheard words in transcripts (that's Transcribe custom vocabulary).

items.name: Topic modeling
items.summary: Discover common topics across a collection of documents without labels.
items.details: An unsupervised technique that groups documents by theme.
items.example: A company discovers the main complaint themes in 100,000 reviews.
items.tip: Discover themes in unlabeled documents → topic modeling (unsupervised).

items.name: Amazon Comprehend Medical
items.summary: Extract medical conditions, medications, dosages, and tests and link them to ICD-10-CM and RxNorm.
items.details: HIPAA-eligible and pre-trained for clinical text.
items.example: A provider structures unstructured clinical notes.
items.tip: Medical text → Comprehend Medical. Medical speech → Transcribe Medical.

sections.title: Amazon Textract
sections.summary: Extract printed and handwritten text, forms, and tables from scanned documents and images.

items.name: Text & handwriting detection
items.summary: OCR for printed and handwritten text in PDFs and images.
items.details: Returns words and lines with their positions and confidence scores.
items.example: Handwritten delivery notes are digitized.
items.tip: Documents → Textract. Text in a street photo → Rekognition text detection.

items.name: Forms & tables
items.summary: Extract key-value pairs and table structure while preserving which value belongs where.
items.details: Goes beyond OCR by understanding document layout.
items.example: Claim forms are turned into structured fields such as policy number and date.
items.tip: Keep which value belongs to which field → forms (key-value pairs) and tables.

items.name: Queries
items.summary: Ask natural-language questions of a document, such as "What is the invoice total?".
items.details: Useful when field locations vary across document layouts.
items.example: A lender extracts the borrower's name from differently formatted applications.
items.tip: Ask a document a question when layouts vary → Textract Queries.

items.name: Expense & ID analysis
items.summary: Specialized extraction for invoices and receipts, and for identity documents.
items.details: Pre-trained for common fields such as vendor, total, and ID number.
items.example: An expense app reads totals and vendors from receipt photos.
items.tip: Invoices, receipts, and ID documents → specialized Textract APIs.

items.name: Human review with A2I
items.summary: Send low-confidence extractions to human reviewers before they're used.
items.details: Textract has built-in integration with Amazon Augmented AI.
items.example: Regulated loan documents are double-checked by people when confidence is low.
items.tip: Human check of low-confidence extractions → A2I with Textract.

sections.title: Amazon Rekognition
sections.summary: Pre-trained image and video analysis: objects, faces, text, unsafe content, and custom labels.

items.name: Object & scene detection
items.summary: Identify objects, scenes, and activities in images and videos.
items.details: Returns labels with confidence scores for things such as vehicles, animals, or buildings.
items.example: A photo library auto-tags images for search.
items.tip: Rekognition ANALYZES images; it does not generate them (that's Nova Canvas via Bedrock).

items.name: Face detection, comparison & search
items.summary: Detect faces, compare them, and search face collections.
items.details: Used for identity verification and access control. Review AWS's AI Service Card for responsible use.
items.example: A building-access system verifies employees by face.
items.tip: Compare a selfie to an ID photo → Rekognition face comparison.

items.name: Content moderation
items.summary: Detect inappropriate or unsafe content in images and videos.
items.details: Flags categories such as explicit or violent content for review.
items.example: A social app screens user-uploaded photos.
items.tip: Unsafe IMAGES or VIDEO → Rekognition moderation. Unsafe GenAI TEXT → Guardrails.

items.name: Text in images
items.summary: Detect text in photos and video frames, such as signs and captions.
items.details: Designed for scene text, not for structured documents or forms.
items.example: A parking system reads text on signs.
items.tip: Text in scene photos → Rekognition. Text in scanned documents → Textract.

items.name: PPE detection
items.summary: Detect whether people are wearing protective equipment such as helmets or masks.
items.details: Supports workplace safety monitoring.
items.example: A construction site checks hard-hat compliance.
items.tip: Helmet or mask compliance from cameras → PPE detection.

items.name: Custom Labels
items.summary: Train a model to recognize your own objects or defects from labeled images.
items.details: Needs labeled images of each category — unlabeled images are not enough.
items.example: A manufacturer detects scratches on its products.
items.tip: "Categorize images by our own categories" → label the images, then train Rekognition Custom Labels.

sections.title: Amazon Transcribe
sections.summary: Automatic speech recognition: convert speech to text, in batch or streaming.

items.name: Batch & streaming transcription
items.summary: Transcribe recorded files or live audio streams.
items.details: Batch suits stored recordings; streaming suits live captions and voice apps.
items.example: Live captions for a webinar use streaming transcription.
items.tip: Live captions → streaming. Recorded files → batch.

items.name: Custom vocabulary
items.summary: Improve recognition of specific words such as product names, acronyms, and jargon.
items.details: The quickest fix when particular terms are misheard.
items.example: Drug names in sales meetings are transcribed correctly.
items.tip: Transcribe custom vocabulary (speech→text) vs Polly lexicon (text→speech) vs Translate custom terminology (translation).

items.name: Custom language models
items.summary: Train Transcribe on domain text to improve accuracy for domain-specific speech overall.
items.details: Better than a vocabulary list when the whole domain language differs (for example medical or legal speech).
items.example: A legal firm improves transcripts of court proceedings.
items.tip: "Improve transcription accuracy for domain-specific speech" → custom language model (or vocabulary for specific terms).

items.name: Speaker diarization
items.summary: Label who spoke when in a multi-speaker recording.
items.details: Separates agent and customer, or multiple meeting participants.
items.example: Meeting notes show which person said what.
items.tip: Who said what in a recording → speaker diarization.

items.name: PII redaction
items.summary: Automatically remove personal data from transcripts.
items.details: Helps meet privacy requirements for stored call transcripts.
items.example: Card numbers spoken on calls never appear in transcripts.
items.tip: Remove card numbers from call transcripts → Transcribe PII redaction.

items.name: Call Analytics
items.summary: Contact-center insights: sentiment, talk time, interruptions, issues, and summaries.
items.details: Built specifically for customer calls.
items.example: Supervisors find calls with negative sentiment and long silences.
items.tip: Contact-center insights (sentiment, talk time, summaries) from calls → Call Analytics.

items.name: Transcribe Medical
items.summary: Speech-to-text tuned for clinical conversations and dictation.
items.details: HIPAA-eligible and trained on medical vocabulary.
items.example: Doctors dictate notes that are transcribed accurately.
items.tip: Clinical dictation to text → Transcribe Medical; then Comprehend Medical for entities.

items.name: Language identification
items.summary: Automatically detect the language spoken in audio.
items.details: Useful for multilingual contact centers. It doesn't improve accuracy for domain jargon.
items.example: Calls in several languages are transcribed without choosing the language first.
items.tip: Language identification doesn't improve accuracy for jargon — that's custom vocabulary or language models.

sections.title: Amazon Translate
sections.summary: Neural machine translation between languages, in real time or in batch.

items.name: Real-time & batch translation
items.summary: Translate text on demand or translate documents in S3 as a batch job.
items.details: Batch translation suits large document collections.
items.example: A retailer translates its product catalog into five languages overnight.
items.tip: Large document collections in S3 → batch translation.

items.name: Custom terminology
items.summary: Control how specific terms, such as brand names, are translated.
items.details: Ensures consistent translation of names and domain terms.
items.example: The brand name is never translated in any language.
items.tip: Brand names must translate consistently (or not at all) → custom terminology.

items.name: Active Custom Translation (parallel data)
items.summary: Adapt translation style and domain using example source-target sentence pairs.
items.details: No model training is needed; examples steer translations at run time.
items.example: Marketing translations adopt the company's informal tone.
items.tip: Match a tone or domain style with example translations → Active Custom Translation.

sections.title: Amazon Polly
sections.summary: Text-to-speech: turn text into lifelike speech in many voices and languages.

items.name: Voices & engines
items.summary: Choose from many voices, with standard, neural, and generative engines.
items.details: Voice quality and naturalness vary by engine.
items.example: An accessibility feature reads news articles aloud.
items.tip: Text → speech is Polly. Speech → text is Transcribe.

items.name: SSML
items.summary: Markup to control pronunciation, pauses, emphasis, and speaking rate per request.
items.details: SSML tags adjust how a specific piece of text is spoken.
items.example: An IVR pauses before reading an account balance.
items.tip: One-off pauses or emphasis → SSML. Pronunciation applied everywhere → lexicon.

items.name: Pronunciation lexicons
items.summary: Define custom pronunciations that apply automatically to all speech you synthesize.
items.details: The fix for brand names or acronyms that Polly mispronounces.
items.example: Invented product names are pronounced correctly in every announcement.
items.tip: Mispronounced brand names in every announcement → Polly lexicon (not Transcribe vocabulary).

items.name: Speech marks
items.summary: Metadata that shows when each word or sentence is spoken, for syncing visuals.
items.details: Used for lip-sync animation or highlighting words as they are read.
items.example: An e-learning app highlights each word as it's spoken.
items.tip: Sync highlighting or lip movement with speech → speech marks.

sections.title: Amazon Lex
sections.summary: Build voice and text chatbots with intents, slots, and fulfillment.

items.name: Intents & utterances
items.summary: An intent is what the user wants; sample utterances teach Lex how users ask for it.
items.details: Lex uses natural language understanding and automatic speech recognition to map input to intents.
items.example: "I lost my card" maps to the ReportLostCard intent.
items.tip: Lex manages the conversation. Transcribe only converts speech to text; Polly only speaks.

items.name: Slots
items.summary: Pieces of information that Lex collects through multi-turn dialog, such as dates or card digits.
items.details: Lex prompts the user for any required slot that is missing.
items.example: The bot asks for the last four digits of the card before continuing.
items.tip: Bot must ask for missing details (dates, card digits) → slots.

items.name: Fulfillment with Lambda
items.summary: Call a Lambda function to validate input or complete the user's request.
items.details: Connects the bot to backend systems.
items.example: The bot calls a Lambda function that blocks the lost card.
items.tip: Bot must take an action in a backend → Lambda fulfillment.

items.name: Channels (web, voice, contact center)
items.summary: Deploy the same bot to websites, messaging apps, and phone lines.
items.details: One bot definition serves text and voice experiences.
items.example: A bank uses the same bot on its website and its phone line.
items.tip: Same bot on web chat and phone → Lex with voice and text channels.

sections.title: Amazon Personalize
sections.summary: Fully managed recommendations from user-item interaction data, in real time.

items.name: Personalized recommendations
items.summary: Recommend items per user based on behavior, updated in real time as they interact.
items.details: No ML expertise needed — you provide interactions, items, and users data.
items.example: A streaming service updates recommended titles while the viewer watches.
items.tip: Recommendations from behavior → Personalize. Semantic document search → Kendra or OpenSearch.

items.name: Similar items & trending
items.summary: Recipes for "customers also viewed", similar items, and popular items.
items.details: Different recipes suit different recommendation scenarios.
items.example: A product page shows similar items.
items.tip: "Customers who viewed this also viewed" → similar-items recipe.

items.name: User segmentation
items.summary: Find users most likely to interact with an item or attribute, for targeted campaigns.
items.details: Useful for marketing audiences.
items.example: Marketing targets users most likely to buy a new product line.
items.tip: Who is likely to buy this? → user segmentation for campaigns.

sections.title: Amazon Kendra
sections.summary: Intelligent enterprise search across document repositories using natural-language questions.

items.name: What Kendra is
items.summary: Semantic search that returns relevant passages and answers from connected enterprise sources.
items.details: Kendra indexes content from many connectors and respects document permissions. It does not give direct FM access.
items.example: Employees search the intranet in plain English and get precise answers.
items.tip: Kendra is a common distractor: it searches documents — it doesn't extract form data (Textract) or host FMs (Bedrock/JumpStart).

sections.title: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)
sections.summary: Control who can access which AWS resources and actions.

items.name: IAM roles & temporary credentials
items.summary: Roles give workloads and users temporary credentials instead of long-lived access keys.
items.details: Applications on EC2, Lambda, or containers should assume a role rather than store keys.
items.example: A Lambda function calls Bedrock using its execution role.
items.tip: Never put access keys in code, prompts, or environment files — use roles.

items.name: Identity-based & resource-based policies
items.summary: JSON policies that allow or deny actions on resources, with optional conditions.
items.details: Identity policies attach to users and roles; resource policies attach to resources such as S3 buckets or KMS keys.
items.example: A policy allows bedrock:InvokeModel only on two approved model ARNs.
items.tip: Restricting which FMs developers can invoke → IAM policy on model ARNs.

items.name: Least privilege
items.summary: Grant only the permissions needed for a task, and nothing more.
items.details: Least privilege limits the damage from mistakes, compromised credentials, and prompt-injected agents.
items.example: A summarization service can only read one S3 prefix.
items.tip: Grant only required actions on specific resources — never administrator access "to avoid errors".

items.name: MFA & root user protection
items.summary: Require multi-factor authentication for human users and avoid using the root user.
items.details: The root user has unrestricted access and should be locked away with MFA.
items.example: Administrators sign in with MFA; the root user is used only for rare account tasks.
items.tip: Stronger protection for human sign-in → MFA. Root user → lock away, avoid daily use.

sections.title: AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS)
sections.summary: Create and control encryption keys used to protect data at rest.

items.name: AWS owned, AWS managed & customer managed keys
items.summary: Customer managed keys give you control of the key policy, rotation, and revocation.
items.details: AWS owned keys are fully managed by AWS; you can't see or control them.
items.example: A company encrypts its custom Bedrock model with a customer managed key it can disable.
items.tip: "We must control and be able to revoke the key" → customer managed KMS key.

items.name: Key policies & auditing
items.summary: Key policies decide who can use a key; every key use is logged in AWS CloudTrail.
items.details: This gives separation of duties between data access and key access.
items.example: Security can prove exactly which role decrypted the training data.
items.tip: Who used a key and when → CloudTrail logs of KMS usage.

items.name: Key rotation
items.summary: Automatically rotate key material on a schedule.
items.details: Rotation limits the exposure of any one version of key material.
items.example: A compliance policy requires yearly rotation of data keys.
items.tip: Scheduled rotation of key material → KMS automatic key rotation.

sections.title: Amazon Macie
sections.summary: Discover and report sensitive data (PII, financial data) stored in Amazon S3.

items.name: Sensitive data discovery
items.summary: Uses ML and pattern matching to find sensitive data across S3 buckets.
items.details: Results appear as findings you can review centrally or send to other services.
items.example: Before building a knowledge base, security finds buckets containing card numbers.
items.tip: PII stored in S3 → Macie. Software vulnerabilities → Inspector. Threats → GuardDuty.

items.name: S3 security posture
items.summary: Also inventories buckets and flags public access or missing encryption.
items.details: Combines data sensitivity with bucket configuration to prioritize risk.
items.example: Macie flags a public bucket that also contains personal data.
items.tip: Public buckets containing sensitive data → Macie findings.

sections.title: Amazon Inspector
sections.summary: Automated vulnerability management for EC2, container images in ECR, and Lambda.

items.name: Continuous vulnerability scanning
items.summary: Finds software vulnerabilities (CVEs) and unintended network exposure, with remediation guidance.
items.details: Scanning is automatic and continuous as new vulnerabilities are published.
items.example: A model-serving container image is flagged for a vulnerable library.
items.tip: Vulnerabilities → Inspector. Configuration compliance → Config. API history → CloudTrail.

sections.title: AWS Artifact
sections.summary: Self-service portal for AWS compliance reports and agreements.

items.name: Compliance reports
items.summary: Download AWS audit reports such as SOC and ISO certifications.
items.details: Auditors use these to assess the controls of AWS as your cloud provider.
items.example: An auditor requests AWS's SOC 2 report.
items.tip: AWS's reports → Artifact. Collect evidence for YOUR controls → AWS Audit Manager.

items.name: Agreements
items.summary: Review and accept agreements such as the Business Associate Addendum (BAA) for HIPAA.
items.details: Needed before processing protected health information on eligible services.
items.example: A healthcare company accepts the BAA before building on Bedrock.
items.tip: HIPAA workloads need the BAA → accept it in AWS Artifact.

sections.title: AWS Secrets Manager
sections.summary: Store, retrieve, and rotate secrets such as API keys and database passwords.

items.name: Store & rotate secrets
items.summary: Applications fetch secrets at run time with IAM permissions; rotation can be automatic.
items.details: Secrets never need to appear in code, prompts, or logs.
items.example: An agent tool retrieves a third-party API key when it runs.
items.tip: Secrets Manager stores secrets; KMS manages encryption keys. Don't put secrets in knowledge bases or prompts.

sections.title: Amazon GuardDuty
sections.summary: Intelligent threat detection that monitors accounts and workloads for malicious activity.

items.name: Threat detection
items.summary: Analyzes logs and activity with ML and threat intelligence to find suspicious behavior.
items.details: Examples include compromised credentials, unusual API calls, and crypto-mining.
items.example: GuardDuty alerts on API calls from a known malicious IP address.
items.tip: Threats in activity → GuardDuty. Vulnerable software → Inspector. Sensitive data → Macie.

sections.title: AWS CloudTrail
sections.summary: Records API activity in your account: who did what, when, and from where.

items.name: Management & data events
items.summary: Logs API calls with the caller identity, time, source IP, and parameters.
items.details: Trails deliver events to Amazon S3 for long-term audit.
items.example: Security finds which role deleted a guardrail over the weekend.
items.tip: CloudTrail doesn't store full prompt/response text — that's Bedrock invocation logging.

sections.title: Amazon CloudWatch
sections.summary: Metrics, logs, alarms, and dashboards for AWS resources and applications.

items.name: Metrics & alarms
items.summary: Track performance metrics and alert or act when thresholds are crossed.
items.details: Bedrock and SageMaker AI publish metrics such as invocations, latency, and errors.
items.example: An alarm notifies the team when model latency exceeds 2 seconds.
items.tip: CloudWatch shows HOW MANY calls and how fast — not WHO made them (CloudTrail).

items.name: CloudWatch Logs
items.summary: Store and query logs, with a retention period you set per log group.
items.details: Bedrock invocation logs can be delivered here; retention settings enforce deletion policies.
items.example: Invocation logs are kept for 90 days, then deleted automatically.
items.tip: Delete logs after N days → set the log group retention period.

sections.title: AWS Config
sections.summary: Tracks resource configurations over time and checks them against rules.

items.name: Configuration history
items.summary: Records how each resource's configuration changed over time.
items.details: Useful for audits and troubleshooting.
items.example: An auditor reviews when a notebook instance's settings changed.
items.tip: "What did this resource's configuration look like last month?" → Config history.

items.name: Config rules & remediation
items.summary: Continuously evaluate resources against managed or custom rules and optionally remediate.
items.details: For example, a managed rule checks that SageMaker notebooks have direct internet access disabled.
items.example: Non-compliant S3 buckets without encryption are flagged automatically.
items.tip: Continuous configuration compliance → Config. Vulnerabilities → Inspector.

items.name: Conformance packs
items.summary: Bundles of Config rules deployed together for a compliance framework.
items.details: Simplifies applying a consistent set of checks across accounts.
items.example: A bank deploys a pack of rules aligned with its security baseline.
items.tip: Deploy a whole set of compliance rules at once → conformance pack.

sections.title: AWS Trusted Advisor
