sections.summary: Automated best-practice checks across cost, security, fault tolerance, performance, and quotas.

items.name: Best-practice checks
items.summary: Inspects your account and recommends improvements.
items.details: Examples: open security groups, idle resources, and service quota usage.
items.example: Trusted Advisor flags an underused instance to cut costs.
items.tip: Account-wide automated recommendations → Trusted Advisor. Question-based workload review → Well-Architected Tool.

sections.title: AWS Well-Architected Tool & lenses
sections.summary: Review workloads against AWS best practices, including generative AI, ML, and responsible AI lenses.

items.name: Well-Architected Tool
items.summary: Answer questions about a workload and get a prioritized improvement plan.
items.details: Covers the six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance, cost, and sustainability.
items.example: An architect reviews a RAG application before launch.
items.tip: Question-based workload review → Well-Architected Tool. Automated account checks → Trusted Advisor.

items.name: Generative AI Lens
items.summary: Best practices for designing and operating generative AI workloads.
items.details: Covers topics such as model selection, prompt management, and responsible use.
items.example: The team checks its chatbot design against the lens.
items.tip: Best-practice guidance for GenAI workloads → Generative AI Lens.

items.name: Responsible AI Lens
items.summary: Best practices for building AI systems responsibly throughout the lifecycle.
items.details: Covers fairness, transparency, privacy, safety, and governance practices.
items.example: A team uses the lens to plan a system card and human oversight.
items.tip: Guidance for building AI responsibly → Responsible AI Lens.

items.name: Machine Learning Lens
items.summary: Best practices across the ML lifecycle, from problem framing to monitoring.
items.details: Useful when designing traditional ML workloads on AWS.
items.example: A team designs its retraining process using the lens.
items.tip: Best practices across the ML lifecycle → Machine Learning Lens.

sections.title: AWS Glue
sections.summary: Serverless data integration: ETL jobs, a data catalog, and data quality.

items.name: ETL jobs
items.summary: Extract, transform, and load data at scale without managing servers.
items.details: Prepares raw data for analytics and ML training.
items.example: Clickstream logs are cleaned and joined before training a model.
items.tip: Serverless ETL to prepare training data → AWS Glue.

items.name: Data Catalog & crawlers
items.summary: Central metadata catalog of datasets; crawlers discover schemas automatically.
items.details: Supports data discovery and governance, and is used by Athena, EMR, and Lake Formation.
items.example: Analysts find the right training table by searching the catalog.
items.tip: A catalog stores metadata about data — it doesn't store vectors or run similarity search.

items.name: Glue Data Quality
items.summary: Define and monitor data quality rules for datasets.
items.details: Catches problems such as missing or out-of-range values before training.
items.example: A pipeline stops if more than 5% of labels are missing.
items.tip: Catch bad data before training → data quality rules.

sections.title: AWS Glue DataBrew
sections.summary: Visual, no-code data preparation with hundreds of built-in transformations.

items.name: What DataBrew is
items.summary: Profile, clean, and normalize data through a visual interface.
items.details: Aimed at analysts who want to prepare data without writing code.
items.example: An analyst standardizes date formats and removes duplicates before analysis.
items.tip: Visual, no-code data cleaning for analysts → DataBrew.

sections.title: AWS Lake Formation
sections.summary: Build and govern data lakes with fine-grained access control.

items.name: Fine-grained permissions
items.summary: Grant access at database, table, column, row, and cell level.
items.details: Lets data scientists use a table while hiding sensitive columns.
items.example: Data scientists query customer data without seeing national ID columns.
items.tip: Column-level access to data lake tables → Lake Formation (not S3 bucket policies or KMS).

sections.title: Amazon EMR
sections.summary: Managed big data platform for Apache Spark, Hive, and other open-source frameworks.

items.name: What EMR is
items.summary: Process very large datasets with open-source frameworks on managed clusters or serverless.
items.details: Used for large-scale data processing and feature engineering.
items.example: Terabytes of logs are processed with Spark to create training features.
items.tip: Big data processing with Spark/Hadoop → EMR.

sections.title: Amazon Redshift
sections.summary: Cloud data warehouse for fast SQL analytics on large structured datasets.

items.name: What Redshift is
items.summary: Petabyte-scale columnar data warehouse for analytics and BI.
items.details: Often the source of structured data for dashboards and ML.
items.example: Finance runs quarterly revenue analysis on Redshift.
items.tip: SQL analytics on large structured data → Redshift (a data warehouse, not a vector store).

items.name: Redshift ML
items.summary: Create and use ML models with SQL commands.
items.details: Uses SageMaker AI behind the scenes so SQL users can train and predict.
items.example: An analyst predicts churn with a CREATE MODEL SQL statement.
items.tip: SQL users building ML models → Redshift ML.

sections.title: Amazon OpenSearch Service
sections.summary: Search and analytics engine that also works as a vector database for RAG.

items.name: Vector (k-NN) search
items.summary: Store embeddings and find the nearest neighbors for semantic search and RAG.
items.details: Supports hybrid search that combines keyword and vector relevance.
items.example: A support portal matches "laptop won't turn on" to "notebook does not power up".
items.tip: Common default vector store for Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

items.name: OpenSearch Serverless vector collections
items.summary: Vector search without managing clusters; capacity scales automatically.
items.details: Bedrock Knowledge Bases can quick-create a collection for you.
items.example: A team launches RAG without sizing a search cluster.
items.tip: Vector search without managing clusters → OpenSearch Serverless vector collection.

sections.title: AWS Data Exchange
sections.summary: Find, subscribe to, and use third-party datasets.

items.name: What Data Exchange is
items.summary: Marketplace for third-party data products delivered to your account.
items.details: Useful for enriching training data, subject to licensing terms.
items.example: A retailer subscribes to weather data to improve demand forecasts.
items.tip: Check licensing and usage rights of third-party data before training.

sections.title: Amazon Aurora & Amazon RDS
sections.summary: Managed relational databases; PostgreSQL editions support vector search with pgvector.

items.name: pgvector on Aurora / RDS for PostgreSQL
items.summary: Store embeddings next to relational data and query similarity with SQL.
items.details: Aurora PostgreSQL can be a Bedrock Knowledge Bases vector store (including quick create).
items.example: A catalog already on Aurora adds semantic search without a new database.
items.tip: "Keep embeddings with existing relational data, use SQL, no new engine" → pgvector.

items.name: Amazon RDS
items.summary: Managed relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, and others) with backups and patching handled.
items.details: RDS for PostgreSQL also supports the pgvector extension.
items.example: An app's transactional data lives in RDS for PostgreSQL.
items.tip: Managed relational database; PostgreSQL + pgvector adds vector search.

sections.title: Amazon DynamoDB
sections.summary: Serverless NoSQL key-value and document database with single-digit millisecond performance.

items.name: What DynamoDB is
items.summary: Fully managed NoSQL database that scales automatically.
items.details: Common for session state, user profiles, and high-scale application data.
items.example: A chatbot stores conversation state per user in DynamoDB.
items.tip: Key-value/NoSQL app data at scale → DynamoDB. Relational + SQL → Aurora/RDS.

items.name: Vector search
items.summary: Native vector indexes and similarity search inside DynamoDB (announced August 2026).
items.details: Store embeddings alongside other item attributes and filter on those attributes.
items.example: An app stores product embeddings with product records in the same table.
items.tip: Newer than the April 2026 exam guide — the exam's classic vector-store answers are OpenSearch, Aurora/RDS PostgreSQL, and Neptune.

sections.title: Amazon DocumentDB
sections.summary: Managed JSON document database compatible with MongoDB; supports vector search.

items.name: What DocumentDB is
items.summary: MongoDB-compatible document database for JSON data, with vector search support.
items.details: Suits teams already using MongoDB APIs.
items.example: A content app stores articles and their embeddings as documents.
items.tip: MongoDB-compatible documents (with vector search) → DocumentDB.

sections.title: Amazon Neptune
sections.summary: Managed graph database; Neptune Analytics powers GraphRAG.

items.name: Graph database
items.summary: Stores entities and relationships for queries that traverse connections.
items.details: Suits fraud rings, knowledge graphs, and recommendation relationships.
items.example: A bank finds accounts linked through shared devices.
items.tip: Relationships and connected data → graph database (Neptune).

items.name: Neptune Analytics & GraphRAG
items.summary: Graph analytics with vector search, used by Bedrock Knowledge Bases for GraphRAG.
items.details: Combines relationship reasoning with semantic retrieval.
items.example: Multi-hop research questions are answered from connected facts.
items.tip: GraphRAG vector store for Bedrock Knowledge Bases → Neptune Analytics.

sections.title: Amazon ElastiCache
sections.summary: Managed in-memory cache (Valkey, Redis OSS, Memcached) for microsecond access.

items.name: What ElastiCache is
items.summary: In-memory caching to speed up applications and reduce database load.
items.details: Can also cache frequent LLM responses to save cost and latency.
items.example: Repeated FAQ answers are served from cache instead of calling the model again.
items.tip: Speed up repeated reads (including repeated LLM answers) → in-memory cache.

sections.title: Amazon EC2
sections.summary: Virtual servers, including GPU and AWS-designed ML chips, for full control of hosting and training.

items.name: Instances
items.summary: Choose instance types and manage the operating system, scaling, and patching yourself.
items.details: Self-hosting models on EC2 gives maximum control but the most operational work.
items.example: A team runs an open-weight model on GPU instances it manages.
items.tip: Least operational overhead is rarely EC2 — prefer managed services such as Bedrock or SageMaker AI.

items.name: Accelerated computing (GPUs)
items.summary: Instances with GPUs for training and inference of deep learning models.
items.details: Used underneath SageMaker AI and for self-managed ML.
items.example: A research team trains a vision model on GPU instances.
items.tip: Self-managed GPU training → EC2; managed training → SageMaker AI.

items.name: AWS Trainium & AWS Inferentia
items.summary: AWS-designed chips: Trainium for cost-efficient training, Inferentia for cost-efficient inference.
items.details: Lower cost and energy per workload can also support sustainability goals.
items.example: A company serves its model on Inferentia-based instances to cut inference cost.
items.tip: Training → Trainium. Inference → Inferentia.

sections.title: AWS Lambda
sections.summary: Run code without servers, triggered by events, billed per request and duration.

items.name: What Lambda is
items.summary: Serverless functions with a maximum run time of 15 minutes per invocation.
items.details: Lambda backs Bedrock agent action groups, Lex fulfillment, and custom chunking.
items.example: A Lambda function looks up an order when the agent calls it.
items.tip: Not suited to hosting long-running agent sessions — see AgentCore Runtime.

sections.title: Amazon ECS & Amazon EKS
sections.summary: Run containerized applications and models with Docker (ECS) or Kubernetes (EKS).

items.name: Amazon ECS
items.summary: AWS-native container orchestration, with Fargate for serverless containers.
items.details: Suits containerized front ends and APIs of AI applications.
items.example: A company runs its chatbot web front end on ECS with Fargate.
items.tip: Run a containerized AI front end without managing servers → ECS with Fargate.

items.name: Amazon EKS
items.summary: Managed Kubernetes for teams standardized on Kubernetes tooling.
items.details: Some teams self-host models on EKS for portability.
items.example: A platform team deploys model servers as Kubernetes workloads.
items.tip: Team standardized on Kubernetes → EKS.

sections.title: Amazon VPC & AWS PrivateLink
sections.summary: Isolated private networks, plus private connectivity to AWS services.

items.name: Virtual private cloud
items.summary: Your own isolated network with subnets, route tables, and security groups.
items.details: Private subnets have no direct internet access.
items.example: Model-serving instances sit in private subnets.
items.tip: Private subnets have no direct internet route; use endpoints for AWS services.

items.name: Interface VPC endpoints (PrivateLink)
items.summary: Private connectivity from your VPC to services such as Bedrock without the public internet.
items.details: Traffic stays on the AWS network, which is often required by security policies.
items.example: A bank's private subnets call Bedrock through an interface endpoint.
items.tip: "No public internet path to Bedrock" → interface endpoint (PrivateLink), not a NAT gateway.

items.name: Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB)
items.summary: Free private route from a VPC to Amazon S3 or DynamoDB.
items.details: Keeps S3 traffic for training data off the internet.
items.example: Training instances read S3 data privately.
items.tip: Private access from a VPC to S3 or DynamoDB → gateway endpoint (free).

items.name: Security groups
items.summary: Virtual firewalls that control inbound and outbound traffic for resources.
items.details: Least-privilege network access for endpoints and databases.
items.example: Only the app tier can reach the vector database port.
items.tip: Restrict which resources can connect to an endpoint or database → security groups.

sections.title: Amazon CloudFront
sections.summary: Content delivery network that serves web content from edge locations.

items.name: What CloudFront is
items.summary: Caches and delivers web content with low latency worldwide.
items.details: It is not a way to connect privately from a VPC to AWS services.
items.example: A chatbot's web front end loads quickly for global users.
items.tip: CloudFront appears as a distractor for private connectivity — that's PrivateLink.

sections.title: Amazon S3
sections.summary: Object storage for training data, knowledge base documents, logs, and model artifacts.

items.name: Buckets & objects
items.summary: Durable storage for any file; the usual home of ML datasets and Bedrock inputs/outputs.
items.details: Knowledge bases, batch inference, fine-tuning jobs, and invocation logs all use S3.
items.example: Fine-tuning data and batch-inference outputs live in S3.
items.tip: Most Bedrock and SageMaker jobs read inputs from and write outputs to S3.

items.name: Access control & encryption
items.summary: Bucket policies, IAM, Block Public Access, and encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS).
items.details: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key gives you control over who can decrypt data.
items.example: Confidential training files are encrypted with a customer managed key.
items.tip: Control who can decrypt training data → SSE-KMS with a customer managed key.

items.name: Versioning & Object Lock
items.summary: Keep previous versions of objects and optionally make them immutable.
items.details: Protects the integrity of source data from accidental or malicious changes.
items.example: A tampered knowledge-base document is restored to its previous version.
items.tip: Integrity: restrict writes + versioning (+ Object Lock for immutability).

items.name: Lifecycle rules
items.summary: Automatically transition objects to cheaper storage or expire (delete) them.
items.details: Enforces retention policies, such as deleting logs after 90 days.
items.example: Prompt logs are deleted automatically after 90 days.
items.tip: Transition keeps data; expiration deletes it.

items.name: Amazon S3 Vectors
items.summary: Low-cost vector storage and querying inside S3, for large vector sets queried infrequently.
items.details: Can be used as a Bedrock Knowledge Bases vector store.
items.example: An archive of billions of embeddings is stored cheaply for occasional search.
items.tip: Lowest-cost storage for huge vector sets queried infrequently → S3 Vectors.

items.name: S3 Glacier storage classes
items.summary: Low-cost archive storage for data you rarely access.
items.details: Retrieval takes longer and costs more than standard storage.
items.example: Old training datasets are archived for compliance.
items.tip: Archive rarely used data cheaply → Glacier classes (retrieval is slower).

sections.title: AWS Budgets & AWS Cost Explorer
sections.summary: Track, analyze, and control spending on AI workloads.

items.name: AWS Cost Explorer
items.summary: Visualize and analyze past costs and usage, and forecast spend.
items.details: Filter by service to see what Bedrock or SageMaker AI is costing.
items.example: The team sees that inference costs doubled last month.
items.tip: Analyze where AI spend went → Cost Explorer.

items.name: AWS Budgets
items.summary: Set cost or usage budgets and get alerts when they are exceeded or forecast to be.
items.details: Budgets can also trigger actions to limit further spending.
items.example: An alert fires when monthly Bedrock spend passes 80% of the budget.
items.tip: Alert before spending passes a limit → AWS Budgets.

items.name: Cost allocation tags
items.summary: Tag resources to attribute costs to teams, projects, or applications.
items.details: Supports chargeback and cost per application metrics.
items.example: Each product team sees the cost of its own AI features.
items.tip: Cost per team or application → cost allocation tags.

sections.title: AI, ML, deep learning, GenAI & agentic AI
sections.summary: How the core AI terms relate to each other.

items.name: AI ⊃ ML ⊃ deep learning ⊃ generative AI
items.summary: ML is a subset of AI; deep learning is a subset of ML; GenAI models are built with deep learning.
items.details: AI is the broad goal of machines performing intelligent tasks. ML learns patterns from data. Deep learning uses multi-layer neural networks. GenAI creates new content.
items.example: An LLM chatbot is still an ML (deep learning) model, so ML governance applies.
items.tip: GenAI is not a separate non-ML technology.

items.name: Agentic AI
items.summary: AI systems that plan steps toward a goal and use tools to act, not just answer.
items.details: Agents combine a model with planning, tools, memory, and feedback from each step.
items.example: An assistant books leave: checks the policy, reads the balance, submits the request, notifies the manager.
items.tip: RAG = answer with retrieved facts. Agent = take actions.

items.name: Neural networks
items.summary: Layers of connected nodes whose weights are learned from data.
items.details: Deep networks learn features automatically from raw data such as images, audio, and text.
items.example: A deep network learns to spot damage in parcel photos without hand-crafted features.
items.tip: Deep learning: more data and compute, less interpretability.

items.name: Computer vision & NLP
items.summary: Computer vision understands images and video; NLP understands and generates human language.
items.details: Both are major application areas of deep learning.
items.example: CV inspects products for scratches; NLP classifies support emails.
items.tip: Images/video → computer vision (Rekognition). Language → NLP (Comprehend, LLMs).

items.name: Model vs algorithm; training vs inference
items.summary: An algorithm is the learning procedure; a model is the trained result used for inference.
items.details: Training learns parameters from data. Inference uses the trained model to make predictions on new data.
items.example: The XGBoost algorithm is trained on loan history to produce a model that scores new applications.
items.tip: Using a trained model to make predictions = inference.

items.name: Parameters vs hyperparameters
items.summary: Parameters (weights) are learned during training; hyperparameters are set before training.
items.details: Examples of hyperparameters: learning rate, number of epochs, tree depth.
items.example: The team tunes the learning rate; the network's weights are learned automatically.
items.tip: Tuning hyperparameters is out of scope to DO, but know what they are.

sections.title: Types of machine learning
sections.summary: Supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and self-supervised learning.

items.name: Supervised learning
items.summary: Learns from labeled examples (input → known output) to predict labels for new data.
items.details: Used for classification and regression when historical outcomes are known.
items.example: Predict churn from customer records labeled with whether they canceled.
items.tip: "Labeled data" or "known outcomes" → supervised.

items.name: Unsupervised learning
items.summary: Finds structure in unlabeled data, such as clusters or anomalies.
items.details: No target labels are needed; the algorithm discovers patterns itself.
items.example: Segment 2 million customers into groups with similar behavior.
items.tip: "No labels" + "find groups" → clustering.

items.name: Reinforcement learning
items.summary: An agent learns actions by trial and error to maximize cumulative reward.
items.details: Needs an environment, actions, and a reward signal.
items.example: A thermostat controller learns settings that minimize energy cost while keeping comfort.
items.tip: Actions + environment + reward → reinforcement learning.

items.name: Self-supervised learning
items.summary: Labels are generated from the data itself, such as predicting the next word.
items.details: This is how foundation models are pre-trained on huge unlabeled text corpora.
items.example: An LLM learns language by predicting the next token in billions of sentences.
items.tip: FM pre-training is self-supervised, not RLHF.

items.name: Semi-supervised learning
items.summary: Combines a small labeled set with a large unlabeled set.
items.details: Useful when labeling is expensive.
items.example: A few thousand labeled images plus a million unlabeled ones train a classifier.
items.tip: Few labels plus many unlabeled examples → semi-supervised.

sections.title: Types of data
sections.summary: Labeled vs unlabeled, structured vs unstructured, tabular, time-series, image, and text.

items.name: Labeled vs unlabeled data
items.summary: Labeled data has the target answer attached; unlabeled data doesn't.
items.details: A label is the value the model learns to predict, not just any human-written text.
items.example: Photos marked "damaged" or "undamaged" are labeled data.
items.tip: A label is the target the model predicts — human-written text isn't automatically a label.

items.name: Structured vs unstructured
items.summary: Structured data fits a schema (tables); unstructured data doesn't (text, images, audio, video).
items.details: Where data is stored doesn't change its type.
items.example: A price table is structured; customer emails are unstructured.
items.tip: Timestamped sensor readings are structured; free-text notes are unstructured.

items.name: Time-series data
items.summary: Values recorded over time where order and timing matter.
items.details: Used for forecasting and anomaly detection.
items.example: Electricity demand recorded every 15 minutes.
items.tip: Order in time matters → time-series (forecasting, anomaly detection).

items.name: Tabular, image & text data
items.summary: Tabular data suits traditional ML; images and text usually suit deep learning.
items.details: Data type strongly influences which approach and service to use.
items.example: Loan records (tabular) → gradient-boosted trees; X-rays (images) → deep learning.
items.tip: Tabular → traditional ML is often best. Images, audio, text → deep learning.

sections.title: ML problem types
sections.summary: Match the business question to the right ML task.

items.name: Regression
items.summary: Predict a continuous number.
items.details: Evaluated with RMSE, MAE, or R².
items.example: Predict the dollar amount of an insurance claim.
items.tip: A probability output doesn't make it regression — look at the target.

items.name: Binary, multiclass & multi-label classification
items.summary: Predict a category: two classes, one of many, or several labels at once.
items.details: Evaluated with accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and AUC.
items.example: Tag an article with every relevant topic (multi-label).
items.tip: One label from many = multiclass. Several at once = multi-label.

items.name: Clustering
items.summary: Group similar records without predefined labels (for example k-means).
items.details: An unsupervised technique for segmentation.
items.example: Discover customer segments for marketing campaigns.
items.tip: PCA reduces features; it doesn't create segments — clustering does.

items.name: Anomaly detection
items.summary: Flag unusual data points compared with normal patterns.
items.details: Works when labeled examples of the unusual cases are rare or change constantly.
items.example: Flag transactions that don't look like a customer's normal behavior.
items.tip: Rare, ever-changing fraud with few labels → anomaly detection.

items.name: Forecasting
items.summary: Predict future values of a time series.
items.details: Uses historical patterns such as trends and seasonality.
items.example: Forecast next week's demand per store.
items.tip: Predict future values of a series → forecasting (regression on time-series data).

items.name: Recommendation
items.summary: Suggest items a user is likely to want based on behavior and similarity.
items.details: Managed on AWS with Amazon Personalize.
items.example: "Customers who watched this also watched…"
items.tip: Personalized item suggestions → recommendation (Amazon Personalize).

sections.title: Types of inferencing
sections.summary: Batch, real-time, asynchronous, and serverless — chosen by latency, payload, and traffic.

items.name: Batch vs real-time
items.summary: Batch scores many records offline; real-time answers each request immediately.
items.details: Choose by whether a user or system is waiting for the answer.
items.example: Nightly churn scores (batch) vs fraud score at checkout (real-time).
items.tip: Someone waiting → real-time. Nobody waiting, huge volume → batch.

items.name: Asynchronous & serverless
items.summary: Asynchronous suits large, slow requests; serverless suits intermittent traffic.
items.details: Both can avoid paying for idle capacity in different ways.
items.example: Video analysis (async); a small internal tool with idle nights (serverless).
items.tip: See SageMaker AI — deploy for the service-specific details.

sections.title: Model fit, bias & variance
sections.summary: Overfitting, underfitting, and the bias-variance trade-off.

items.name: Overfitting (high variance)
items.summary: Great on training data, poor on new data — the model memorized noise.
items.details: Fix with more diverse data, regularization, early stopping, or a simpler model.
items.example: 99% training accuracy, 72% validation accuracy.
items.tip: Training more epochs or adding layers makes overfitting worse.

items.name: Underfitting (high bias)
items.summary: Poor on both training and new data — the model is too simple.
items.details: Fix with more informative features, a more expressive model, or more training.
items.example: A linear model can't capture the patterns in delivery times.
items.tip: Poor on training AND validation → underfitting (high bias).

items.name: Bias-variance trade-off
items.summary: Reducing bias often increases variance and vice versa; aim for good generalization.
items.details: Bias and variance can also differ by subgroup, affecting fairness.
items.example: A model underfits a small rural group that had too little training data.
items.tip: Aim for a model that generalizes — neither memorizing nor oversimplifying.

items.name: Data leakage
items.summary: Training uses information that won't be available at prediction time, inflating results.
items.details: Leaked features make offline accuracy look excellent but fail in production.
items.example: A loan model uses a field filled in only after a borrower defaults.
items.tip: Suspiciously excellent offline accuracy → suspect data leakage.

items.name: Train, validation & test sets
items.summary: Train on one set, tune on another, and report final performance on an untouched test set.
items.details: Tuning on the test set produces over-optimistic results.
items.example: The team holds out 15% of data that is never used for tuning.
items.tip: Never tune on the test set — it must stay an honest estimate.

sections.title: ML development lifecycle & pipeline
sections.summary: The stages from business problem to monitoring, and the AWS services for each.

items.name: Lifecycle stages in order
items.summary: Frame problem → collect data → prepare & engineer features → train & tune → evaluate → deploy → monitor.
items.details: Monitoring feeds back into retraining, making the lifecycle a loop.
items.example: A churn project follows these stages and retrains when drift appears.
items.tip: Watch for ordering questions: evaluation comes before deployment; monitoring after.

items.name: EDA & feature engineering
items.summary: Explore data to understand it, then create or transform variables that help the model.
items.details: Feature engineering can add variables, such as "days since last purchase".
items.example: A team adds seasonal features to improve a demand model.
items.tip: "Increase the number of variables" → data collection and feature engineering, not hyperparameter tuning.

items.name: AWS services by stage
items.summary: Data: Glue, DataBrew, Data Wrangler, Ground Truth. Train: SageMaker AI. Deploy/monitor: endpoints, Model Monitor.
items.details: Governance spans the lifecycle: Model Registry, Model Cards, Clarify, lineage tracking.
items.example: Labels from Ground Truth → training job → registry → endpoint → Model Monitor.
items.tip: Label data → Ground Truth. Features → Feature Store. Monitor → Model Monitor.

items.name: Sources of models
items.summary: Use a pre-trained model (API or open weights) or train a custom one.
items.details: Managed APIs (Bedrock) are fastest; open models (JumpStart) give control; custom training gives the most control at the highest cost.
items.example: A team starts with Bedrock, later self-hosts an open model for control.
items.tip: Fastest start → managed API. Control → open model you host. Most control, most cost → custom training.

sections.title: MLOps & drift
sections.summary: Make ML repeatable, scalable, monitored, and maintainable in production.

items.name: MLOps practices
items.summary: Versioned data and code, automated pipelines, a model registry, monitoring, and retraining.
items.details: MLOps reduces technical debt and makes models reproducible and production-ready.
items.example: Every model can be rebuilt from its pipeline run and registered version.
items.tip: "Can't reproduce last year's model" → versioned pipelines + model registry.

items.name: Data drift
items.summary: Input data distributions change from the training baseline.
items.details: Detected by comparing live inputs with the baseline (SageMaker Model Monitor).
items.example: A new product attracts younger customers than the training data had.
items.tip: Response to drift: retrain on recent, representative data — not rollback or bigger instances.

items.name: Concept drift
items.summary: The relationship between inputs and the target changes, even if inputs look the same.
items.details: Detected by monitoring model quality against ground-truth labels.
items.example: Fraudsters change tactics, so the same features now mean fraud more often.
items.tip: Inputs look the same but outcomes changed → concept drift.

items.name: Retraining triggers
items.summary: Retrain on schedule or when monitoring shows drift or quality drop, then evaluate before deploying.
items.details: Evaluation gates prevent a worse model from replacing a better one.
items.example: Retraining runs when accuracy falls below target, and deploys only if the new model wins.
items.tip: Retrain on recent data, evaluate against production, then redeploy.

sections.title: Model evaluation metrics
sections.summary: Classification and regression metrics — and when each matters.

items.name: Accuracy
items.summary: Share of all predictions that are correct.
items.details: Misleading with imbalanced classes.
items.example: A model that never flags fraud is 99.5% accurate when 0.5% is fraud.
items.tip: Imbalanced data → don't trust accuracy.

items.name: Precision
items.summary: Of the items flagged positive, how many really are positive.
items.details: Prioritize when false positives are costly.
items.example: A spam filter that must not send real emails to spam.
items.tip: Costly false alarms → precision.

items.name: Recall (sensitivity)
items.summary: Of all actual positives, how many the model found.
items.details: Prioritize when false negatives (misses) are costly.
items.example: Screening X-rays for disease — missing a case is worst.
items.tip: Costly misses → recall. Costly false alarms → precision.

items.name: F1 score
items.summary: Harmonic mean of precision and recall.
items.details: A single metric that balances both errors, useful with imbalanced classes.
items.example: Fraud detection where both missed fraud and false alarms are costly.
items.tip: Both errors matter + imbalanced classes → F1.

items.name: Confusion matrix & AUC
items.summary: The confusion matrix counts TP, FP, TN, FN; AUC measures class separation across thresholds.
items.details: Both summarize classifier behavior in aggregate.
items.example: The team compares AUC to choose between two fraud models.
items.tip: AUC and the confusion matrix are classification tools.

items.name: RMSE, MAE & R²
items.summary: Error metrics for predicting numbers.
items.details: RMSE penalizes large errors more; MAE is the average absolute error; R² is variance explained.
items.example: An insurer reports claim-amount predictions are off by $420 on average (MAE).
items.tip: F1, precision, recall, and AUC do NOT apply to regression.

sections.title: Business value & ROI of ML
sections.summary: Measure whether ML delivers value, not just technical accuracy.

items.name: Business metrics
items.summary: Cost per user or task, development cost, customer feedback, time saved, revenue, ROI.
items.details: Better model metrics don't guarantee business value.
items.example: F1 improved, but leadership asks whether cost per ticket fell.
items.tip: "Is the project delivering value?" → business metrics, not F1 or validation loss.

items.name: Return on investment
items.summary: Value gained (time saved, revenue, errors avoided) compared with total cost.
items.details: Include development, inference, monitoring, and maintenance costs.
items.example: A routing model saves 2,000 agent hours per year versus its running cost.
items.tip: ROI weighs value delivered against ALL costs, including maintenance.

sections.title: When to use AI/ML — and when not to
sections.summary: Use cases where ML adds value, and when rules, cost, or explainability rule it out.

items.name: Where ML adds value
items.summary: Scale, automation, and assisting human decisions on patterns too complex for rules.
items.details: Examples: fraud detection, forecasting, recommendations, computer vision, NLP.
items.example: Thousands of daily documents are classified automatically.
items.tip: ML helps with scale, automation, and patterns too complex for rules.

items.name: When ML is not appropriate
items.summary: When exact, deterministic outcomes are required or the cost exceeds the benefit.
items.details: ML produces predictions, not guarantees. Known formulas belong in conventional code.
items.example: Calculating a legally defined benefit amount.
items.tip: "A specific outcome is needed instead of a prediction" → don't use ML.

items.name: Traditional ML vs foundation models
items.summary: Traditional ML: narrow, structured, explainable, low-latency. FMs: open-ended, unstructured, generative.
items.details: Regulatory explainability, strict latency, or tabular data favor traditional ML.
items.example: Loan decisions with required reasons → traditional model with feature attributions.
items.tip: Explainability rules or millisecond latency on tabular data → traditional ML.

sections.title: GenAI building blocks
sections.summary: Tokens, embeddings, vectors, chunking, and prompts.

items.name: Tokens
items.summary: The units a model reads and writes — whole words, word pieces, or punctuation.
items.details: Each model has its own tokenizer, so the same text can have different token counts.
items.example: 750 words become about 1,000 tokens on one model and a different count on another.
items.tip: Tokens ≠ words. Pricing and limits are in tokens.

items.name: Embeddings & vectors
items.summary: Numeric representations where similar meaning means nearby vectors.
items.details: Used for semantic search, RAG retrieval, clustering, and recommendations.
items.example: "Laptop won't turn on" matches "notebook does not power up".
items.tip: Match by meaning, not keywords → embeddings + vector similarity.

items.name: Chunking
items.summary: Splitting documents into smaller passages before embedding them.
items.details: Chunk size trades precision for context.
items.example: Manuals are split so that each chunk covers one procedure.
items.tip: Missing context in answers → chunks too small; irrelevant noise → chunks too big.

items.name: Vector databases
items.summary: Stores that index embeddings for fast similarity search.
items.details: On AWS: OpenSearch, Aurora/RDS PostgreSQL (pgvector), Neptune Analytics, DocumentDB, S3 Vectors, and more.
items.example: A RAG app retrieves the 5 most similar chunks for each question.
items.tip: A data catalog or permissions service is not a vector store.

items.name: Prompts & prompt engineering
items.summary: The instructions and context sent to a model, and the practice of designing them well.
items.details: Changing the prompt changes behavior without retraining.
items.example: Adding examples and a format makes summaries consistent.
items.tip: Prompting changes behavior without changing model weights.

sections.title: Model types & architectures
sections.summary: Transformers, LLMs, foundation models, diffusion, and multimodal models.

items.name: Foundation models
items.summary: Large models pre-trained on broad data that adapt to many tasks.
items.details: One FM can summarize, translate, answer questions, and write code through prompting.
items.example: A single model powers drafting, summarizing, and Q&A features.
items.tip: FM = large, general-purpose, pre-trained on diverse data, adaptable to many tasks.

items.name: Large language models (LLMs)
items.summary: FMs specialized in understanding and generating language.
items.details: Most LLMs are transformer-based and generate text one token at a time.
items.example: A support assistant drafts replies to customer emails.
items.tip: LLMs generate text token by token; they aren't calculators or databases.

items.name: Transformers & self-attention
items.summary: Self-attention relates every token to every other token and allows parallel training.
items.details: RNNs process tokens sequentially; transformers process the whole sequence together.
items.example: A model resolves which noun "it" refers to across a long paragraph.
items.tip: Self-attention is the key transformer mechanism.

items.name: Diffusion models
items.summary: Generate images by starting from noise and removing it step by step, guided by a prompt.
items.details: Different from GANs, which pit a generator against a discriminator.
items.example: Product images generated from text descriptions.
items.tip: Noise → step-by-step denoising → diffusion model.

items.name: Multimodal models
items.summary: Accept or produce more than one type of data, such as images and text.
items.details: Match the model's input and output modalities to the task.
items.example: A photo of car damage plus a description returns a written assessment.
items.tip: Image + text in, text out → multimodal model.

sections.title: Foundation model lifecycle
sections.summary: Data selection → model selection → pre-training → fine-tuning → evaluation → deployment → feedback.

items.name: Lifecycle order
items.summary: Data selection, model selection, pre-training, fine-tuning, evaluation, deployment, feedback.
items.details: Feedback from production loops back into further improvement.
items.example: A provider pre-trains, then fine-tunes, then evaluates before release.
items.tip: Ordering questions: evaluation comes before deployment; feedback comes last.

items.name: Pre-training
items.summary: Learning general capabilities from massive unlabeled data — the most expensive stage.
items.details: Usually done by model providers; customers typically adapt existing models.
items.example: A lab trains a new model on trillions of tokens across thousands of chips.
items.tip: Pre-training needs the most data, compute, and cost of any stage.

sections.title: GenAI capabilities & limitations
sections.summary: What GenAI does well, and the limitations you must design around.

items.name: Advantages
items.summary: Adaptability, responsiveness, conversational interaction, and content generation.
items.details: One pre-trained model can handle many tasks without task-specific training.
items.example: A single assistant drafts, summarizes, and translates.
items.tip: "One model, many tasks" → adaptability.

items.name: Common use cases
items.summary: Summarization, drafting, chat assistants, translation, code, search, image/audio/video generation.
items.details: Prediction on structured data or exact rules usually belong to other tools.
items.example: Summarizing support conversations for the next agent.
items.tip: Creating or transforming content → GenAI. Predicting numbers → traditional ML.

items.name: Hallucination
items.summary: Fluent, confident output that is false or unsupported.
items.details: Mitigate with grounding (RAG), grounding checks, output validation, and citations.
items.example: A chatbot invents a 60-day return window.
items.tip: Confident but false or unsupported → hallucination.

items.name: Nondeterminism
items.summary: The same prompt can produce different outputs because of sampling.
items.details: Lower temperature and top-p reduce variation.
items.example: Ten runs of the same prompt give ten different product descriptions.
items.tip: Same prompt, different output → sampling; lower temperature.

items.name: Limited interpretability
items.summary: It's hard to trace why an LLM produced an output; its self-explanations may not be faithful.
items.details: When regulators require faithful explanations, prefer interpretable models.
items.example: A bank can't justify loan recommendations from an LLM's reasoning.
items.tip: Faithful explanations required → interpretable model, not an LLM's self-explanation.

items.name: Knowledge cutoff
items.summary: A model knows only what was in its training data, up to a date.
items.details: Supply current or private facts at inference time through RAG or tools.
items.example: A model doesn't know about a regulation from last week.
items.tip: Recent or private facts → RAG or tools, not a lower temperature.

items.name: Bias & inaccuracy
items.summary: Outputs can reflect bias in training data or simply be wrong.
items.details: Human review and evaluation remain necessary for important content.
items.example: Generated product descriptions need editorial review before publishing.
items.tip: Generated content may need human review before publishing.

sections.title: Selecting a foundation model
sections.summary: Criteria: modality, quality, latency, cost, context length, languages, customization, Region.

items.name: Selection criteria
items.summary: Modality, task quality, latency, cost, input/output length, languages, customization, compliance.
items.details: Test candidates on your own representative requests.
items.example: A voice app picks the smallest model that meets quality for sub-second replies.
items.tip: Smallest model that meets the measured requirement usually wins.

items.name: Benchmarks vs your data
items.summary: Public benchmarks narrow the shortlist; your own evaluation decides.
items.details: A top benchmark score doesn't guarantee performance on domain-specific tasks.
items.example: A leaderboard winner performs poorly on internal claims questions.
items.tip: Top benchmark ≠ best for your task; evaluate on your data.

items.name: Regional availability & compliance
items.summary: Models and features vary by Region; residency rules constrain where inference runs.
items.details: Cross-Region inference with a geographic profile keeps processing in one geography.
items.example: An EU company picks a model available in EU Regions.
items.tip: Model not in your Region, or residency rules → check availability and geographic inference profiles.

sections.title: Token pricing & cost levers
sections.summary: How GenAI inference is priced and how to reduce cost.

items.name: Token-based pricing
items.summary: Pay per input token and per output token; output tokens usually cost more.
items.details: Long prompts, large retrieved contexts, and long answers all add cost.
items.example: A 4,000-token document plus a 300-token summary is billed on both counts.
items.tip: Cost = input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price.

items.name: Cost levers
items.summary: Shorter prompts, focused retrieval, output limits, prompt caching, smaller models, batch, routing.
items.details: Match the lever to the cost driver.
items.example: Retrieving 5 relevant chunks instead of whole documents cuts input tokens.
items.tip: Temperature does not change cost or length.

items.name: On-demand vs batch vs Provisioned Throughput
items.summary: Variable traffic → on-demand; offline bulk → batch; steady high volume → Provisioned Throughput.
items.details: Commitments pay off only with consistent utilization.
items.example: A one-time archive job uses batch, not a 6-month commitment.
items.tip: Commitment only pays off with steady, high utilization.

sections.title: Agentic AI concepts
sections.summary: Tools, MCP, memory, multi-agent patterns, orchestration, and context engineering.

items.name: Tool use
items.summary: Agents call tools (APIs, code, databases) to get live data or take actions.
items.details: Tools provide exact results and real actions that token prediction can't.
items.example: An agent calls an order API to get the real delivery status.
items.tip: Live data or real actions → a tool, not a bigger model.

items.name: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
items.summary: Open standard for connecting agents to tools and data sources.
items.details: MCP servers expose tools; agents discover and call them through a common protocol.
items.example: The same ticketing tool works with agents built on different frameworks.
items.tip: MCP = agent ↔ tools/data. A2A = agent ↔ agent.

items.name: Agent-to-agent communication (A2A)
items.summary: Protocols and patterns for agents to delegate work and exchange results.
items.details: Used in multi-agent systems where specialists collaborate.
items.example: A supervisor agent asks a research agent for data.
items.tip: Agents talking to agents → A2A. Agents to tools → MCP.

items.name: Short-term vs long-term memory
items.summary: Short-term memory covers the current session; long-term memory persists facts across sessions.
items.details: Long-term memory stores extracted facts, not whole transcripts.
items.example: An assistant remembers a user's preferred report format next month.
items.tip: Current conversation → short-term. Preferences next month → long-term.

items.name: Multi-agent patterns
items.summary: Supervisor (hierarchical), swarm (peer), graph, and sequential workflow patterns.
items.details: More agents add coordination cost; each needs a clear responsibility.
items.example: A supervisor delegates retrieval and analysis to two specialists.
items.tip: More agents = more coordination, latency, and tokens; still needs evaluation.

items.name: Workflows vs autonomous agents
items.summary: Fixed, auditable steps → orchestrated workflow; unknown path → agent.
items.details: Workflows are predictable; agents are flexible but less predictable.
items.example: Invoice processing always follows four steps, so it runs as a workflow.
items.tip: Predictable, auditable steps → workflow, not an autonomous agent.

items.name: Context engineering
items.summary: Curating what goes into each model call: instructions, relevant data, memory, tool results.
items.details: More context isn't always better — irrelevant context raises cost and distracts the model.
items.example: A long-running agent summarizes old turns and retrieves only what each step needs.
items.tip: Slow, costly, unfocused long sessions → prune/summarize context, not a bigger window.

sections.title: GenAI business value & metrics
sections.summary: How to measure whether a GenAI application pays off.

items.name: Business metrics for GenAI
items.summary: Conversion rate, average revenue per user, customer lifetime value, efficiency, ROI, accuracy.
items.details: Tie metrics to the goal and compare with a control group where possible.
items.example: New product descriptions are A/B tested for conversion rate.
items.tip: Business outcome questions → business metrics, not BLEU or token counts.

items.name: Advantages of AWS GenAI services
items.summary: Lower barrier to entry, speed to market, no infrastructure, security, and compliance programs.
items.details: Customers still own evaluation, data protection, and cost optimization.
items.example: A startup ships a feature in weeks using Bedrock.
items.tip: Managed services speed delivery but don't remove your security or evaluation duties.

sections.title: Customization approaches & cost trade-offs
sections.summary: Prompting, RAG, fine-tuning, continued pre-training, distillation, and pre-training.

items.name: Cost order (lowest → highest)
items.summary: Prompt engineering → RAG → fine-tuning → continued pre-training → pre-training from scratch.
items.details: Start with the cheapest approach that could work and move up only when needed.
items.example: A demo next week starts with a clear prompt, not a training job.
items.tip: Try the cheapest option first: prompt → RAG → fine-tune → continued pre-train → pre-train.

items.name: In-context learning
items.summary: Improve behavior with instructions and examples in the prompt — no weight changes.
items.details: Few-shot prompting is the common form of in-context learning.
items.example: Five example product descriptions teach the model the brand's style.
items.tip: "Least operational effort" for style/format → few-shot prompting.

items.name: RAG vs fine-tuning
items.summary: RAG supplies changing facts at query time; fine-tuning teaches stable behavior or style.
items.details: RAG costs per query (retrieval + input tokens); fine-tuning costs up front and must be repeated.
items.example: Daily-changing prices → RAG; strict letter format → fine-tuning.
items.tip: Frequently changing facts → RAG. Consistent style → fine-tuning.

items.name: Continued (domain-adaptive) pre-training
items.summary: Further pre-train a model on large unlabeled domain text to learn its language.
items.details: Uses unlabeled data, unlike supervised fine-tuning.
items.example: A semiconductor firm adapts a model to its proprietary terminology.
items.tip: Unlabeled domain corpus → continued pre-training. Labeled pairs → fine-tuning.

items.name: Distillation
items.summary: Train a smaller student model on a larger teacher model's outputs.
items.details: Keeps much of the quality at lower cost and latency.
items.example: A claims model runs on a small, fast student at production volume.
items.tip: Cheaper, faster model with near-teacher quality → distillation.

sections.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)
sections.summary: Ground model answers in retrieved documents at query time.

items.name: How RAG works
items.summary: Ingest → chunk → embed → store; at query time: embed question → retrieve → augment prompt → generate.
items.details: The model answers from retrieved context rather than only from training data.
items.example: An assistant answers from this morning's updated policy.
items.tip: Retrieval happens at query time, so no retraining is needed for new facts.

items.name: Why use RAG
items.summary: Current and private facts, source citations, fewer hallucinations, and no retraining.
items.details: Updating knowledge only requires re-indexing documents.
items.example: Weekly policy changes flow into answers after a sync.
items.tip: RAG + citations is also a grounding technique for hallucination reduction.

items.name: Retrieval quality levers
items.summary: Chunking, embeddings model, metadata filters, hybrid search, and reranking.
items.details: Most RAG failures are retrieval failures — check the retrieved passages first.
items.example: Wrong manual versions are fixed with a metadata filter.
items.tip: Fluent answer about the wrong product → fix retrieval first.

sections.title: Inference parameters
sections.summary: Settings that control randomness, length, and stopping of model output.

items.name: Temperature
items.summary: Lower = more deterministic and focused; higher = more varied and creative.
items.details: Use low values for classification and factual answers; higher for brainstorming.
items.example: An email router uses temperature 0 for consistent categories.
items.tip: Temperature doesn't change cost, speed, or knowledge.

items.name: Top-p (nucleus sampling)
items.summary: Sample only from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p.
items.details: Lower top-p narrows choices and reduces randomness.
items.example: Lowering top-p makes product descriptions less erratic.
items.tip: Lower top-p → fewer candidate tokens → less randomness.

items.name: Top-k
items.summary: Sample only from the k most likely next tokens; k = 1 is greedy decoding.
items.details: Smaller k = less variety.
items.example: top_k = 1 makes output nearly deterministic.
items.tip: top_k = 1 → always the most likely token.

items.name: Maximum output tokens
items.summary: Caps response length; stop reason max_tokens means the limit was hit.
items.details: Raise it (within the model's limit) if answers are cut off; lower it to control cost.
items.example: Summaries stop mid-sentence until the limit is raised.
items.tip: The context window covers input + output; raising max output leaves less room for input.

items.name: Stop sequences
items.summary: Strings that end generation when the model produces them.
items.details: Useful for turn-taking and structured output.
items.example: A stop sequence of "User:" stops the model inventing the user's next turn.
items.tip: Model keeps writing past where it should stop → stop sequence.

items.name: Context window
items.summary: Maximum tokens (input + output) a model handles in one request.
items.details: Larger documents need chunking and retrieval, summarization, or a longer-context model.
items.example: A 1,200-page filing is chunked and retrieved rather than sent whole.
items.tip: Document bigger than the context window → chunk and retrieve.

sections.title: Prompt engineering techniques
sections.summary: Zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, templates, and negative prompts.

items.name: Zero-shot prompting
items.summary: Instructions only, no examples.
items.details: Works for simple, well-known tasks.
items.example: "Classify this ticket as Billing, Technical, or Account."
items.tip: Count the examples: 0 = zero-shot, 1 = one-shot, several = few-shot.

items.name: One-shot (single-shot) prompting
items.summary: One example shows the desired pattern or format.
items.details: Useful to demonstrate an exact output format.
items.example: One correctly formatted title, then a new product's attributes.
items.tip: Exactly one example → one-shot (single-shot).

items.name: Few-shot prompting
items.summary: Several labeled examples teach the task, including edge cases.
items.details: Improves consistency without training.
items.example: Labeled reviews teach the company's definition of "mixed" sentiment.
items.tip: Several labeled examples in the prompt → few-shot (in-context learning).

items.name: Chain-of-thought prompting
items.summary: Ask the model to reason step by step before answering.
items.details: Improves multi-step reasoning tasks.
items.example: A shipping-cost question with weight tiers and discounts.
items.tip: For exact math at scale, give the model a code tool instead.

items.name: Prompt templates
items.summary: Fixed instructions and format with variables for changing input.
items.details: Standardizes outputs across many users and requests.
items.example: Every meeting summary uses the same template.
items.tip: Same instructions, different input each time → template with variables.

items.name: Negative prompts
items.summary: Tell the model what to avoid — especially in image generation.
items.details: Image models accept negative text; text prompts use explicit "do not" constraints.
items.example: Banner images exclude text and watermarks.
items.tip: Exclude elements from generated images → negative prompt.

sections.title: Prompt anatomy & best practices
sections.summary: Elements of a good prompt and how to improve it.

items.name: Prompt elements
items.summary: Context (role/background), instruction (task), input data, and output indicator (format).
items.details: Clear separation of elements reduces ambiguity.
items.example: "You are a support analyst…" is context; "Summarize in one sentence" is the instruction.
items.tip: Role = context. Task = instruction. Data = input. Format = output indicator.

items.name: Specificity & concision
items.summary: State the audience, length, and format explicitly; avoid vague requests.
items.details: Specific prompts reduce long, generic answers.
items.example: "Three bullets for executives, under 50 words."
items.tip: Vague, long answers → specify audience, length, and format.

items.name: Delimiters
items.summary: Separate instructions from input content with tags or markers.
items.details: Helps the model distinguish what to do from what to analyze.
items.example: The customer email is wrapped in <email> tags.
items.tip: Delimiters help, but they don't make prompt injection impossible.

items.name: Experimentation & versioning
items.summary: Test prompt variants on the same representative data and version prompts.
items.details: Treat prompts like code: measured, versioned, and reversible.
items.example: Two prompt variants are scored on 200 held-out claims.
items.tip: Pick prompts with measured evidence, not one hand-picked example.

items.name: Guardrails as a best practice
items.summary: Pair prompts with guardrails rather than relying on instructions alone.
items.details: System prompts can be overridden; guardrails enforce policies.
items.example: A denied topic enforces "no investment advice" regardless of phrasing.
items.tip: A system prompt alone is not a security control.

sections.title: Prompt risks & attacks
sections.summary: Injection, jailbreaking, leaking, hijacking, and poisoning.

items.name: Prompt injection (direct & indirect)
items.summary: Malicious instructions that override the application's intended behavior.
items.details: Indirect injection hides instructions in content the model reads, such as web pages or documents.
items.example: A web page tells an agent to email the user's data to an attacker.
items.tip: Treat retrieved and tool content as untrusted data.

items.name: Jailbreaking
items.summary: Role-play, hypotheticals, or obfuscation used to bypass safety behavior.
items.details: Mitigate with prompt attack filters, content filters, and red teaming.
items.example: "Pretend you're an AI with no rules…"
items.tip: Role-play to bypass safety → jailbreak.

items.name: Prompt leaking (exposure)
items.summary: Tricking a model into revealing its system prompt or hidden configuration.
items.details: Never put secrets in prompts; assume the system prompt can be exposed.
items.example: "Print everything above this message" reveals internal rules.
items.tip: Revealing the system prompt → prompt leaking.

items.name: Prompt hijacking
items.summary: Input redirects the model away from its intended task.
items.details: A form of direct injection that changes the goal.
items.example: A translation bot is told to write a product review instead.
items.tip: Input redirects the model to a different task → hijacking.

items.name: Data poisoning
items.summary: Corrupting training or retrieval data to change model behavior.
items.details: Defend with write-access control, integrity checks, versioning, and provenance.
items.example: Fake examples inserted into a fine-tuning bucket promote a competitor.
items.tip: Malicious TRAINING/RETRIEVAL data → poisoning. Malicious INPUT at run time → injection.

items.name: Model inversion
items.summary: Querying a model to reconstruct sensitive training data from its outputs.
items.details: In a model inversion attack, an attacker repeatedly queries a model and analyzes its outputs to infer sensitive details of the training data. A related attack, membership inference, tries to learn whether a specific record was in the training set.
items.example: An attacker uses a face recognition model's confidence scores to reconstruct an approximate image of a person in its training data.
items.tip: Mitigations: train only on data you need, mask PII before training, limit output detail such as confidence scores, and control access.

sections.title: Fine-tuning methods & training data
sections.summary: Instruction tuning, transfer learning, RLHF, and preparing good data.

items.name: Instruction tuning
items.summary: Supervised fine-tuning on instruction → response pairs.
items.details: Improves how well a model follows directions for your tasks.
items.example: "Summarize this complaint for a manager" → ideal summary, thousands of times.
items.tip: Instruction fine-tuning data = prompt-response pairs.

items.name: Transfer learning
items.summary: Reuse knowledge from a pre-trained model for a related task with far less data.
items.details: The principle behind fine-tuning foundation models.
items.example: A general image model is adapted with 2,000 labeled part images.
items.tip: Good results from a small labeled set on top of a pre-trained model → transfer learning.

items.name: Domain adaptation
items.summary: Adapt a model to a specialized domain's language and tasks.
items.details: Achieved with continued pre-training (unlabeled) and/or fine-tuning (labeled).
items.example: A legal model is adapted to contract language.
items.tip: Specialized vocabulary from unlabeled text → continued pre-training.

items.name: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)
items.summary: Human preference rankings train a reward model that guides further training.
items.details: Aligns responses with human judgments of helpfulness and harmlessness.
items.example: Reviewers pick the better of two answers thousands of times.
items.tip: RLHF is training. LLM-as-a-judge is evaluation.

items.name: Data curation & quality
items.summary: Accurate, consistent, representative examples beat large, noisy datasets.
items.details: Remove incorrect or off-brand examples and cover every case the model will see.
items.example: 800 expert-reviewed examples outperform 60,000 inconsistent ones.
items.tip: Quality beats quantity for fine-tuning data.

items.name: Data governance for training
items.summary: Confirm usage rights, minimize or mask personal data, and track provenance.
items.details: Data used for training is hard to remove from a model later.
items.example: Chat transcripts are de-identified before fine-tuning.
items.tip: Embeddings are not anonymization.

sections.title: Evaluating foundation models
sections.summary: Metrics and approaches for judging FM output quality.

items.name: ROUGE
items.summary: Recall-oriented n-gram overlap with reference text — typical for summarization.
items.details: Measures how much of the reference appears in the output.
items.example: Generated case summaries are compared with human summaries.
items.tip: Summarization → ROUGE. Translation → BLEU.

items.name: BLEU
items.summary: Precision-oriented n-gram overlap with reference translations — typical for translation.
items.details: Standard automatic metric for machine translation.
items.example: German manual translations are scored against professional references.
items.tip: Translation quality against references → BLEU.

items.name: BERTScore
items.summary: Compares meaning using contextual embeddings, so paraphrases score well.
items.details: Better than n-gram overlap when wording differs but meaning is the same.
items.example: "No charge if you cancel anytime" matches "cancel at any time without a fee".
items.tip: Same meaning, different words → BERTScore.

items.name: LLM-as-a-judge
items.summary: A model scores outputs against a rubric; scales without reference answers.
items.details: Calibrate with periodic human review.
items.example: 20,000 weekly responses are scored for helpfulness and tone.
items.tip: Large volume, subjective criteria, no references → LLM-as-a-judge.

items.name: Human-in-the-loop evaluation
items.summary: People rate outputs for subjective or expert criteria.
items.details: Slower and costlier but captures nuance automatic metrics miss.
items.example: Copy editors judge brand voice.
items.tip: Nuanced, expert, or brand-specific quality → human evaluation.

items.name: Benchmark datasets
items.summary: Standard datasets for comparing general model capabilities.
items.details: Useful for shortlisting, but they may not reflect your domain or tasks.
items.example: A team shortlists three models by benchmark, then tests them on its own data.
items.tip: Benchmarks narrow choices; your own data decides.

items.name: Perplexity
items.summary: How well a language model predicts a sample of text. Lower is better.
items.details: Perplexity is calculated from the probabilities a model assigns to each token in held-out text. It is useful for comparing language models on the same data, but it doesn't measure factual accuracy or helpfulness.
items.example: After continued pre-training on legal documents, perplexity on held-out legal text falls, showing that the model fits the domain better.
items.tip: Lower perplexity is better. Unlike ROUGE or BLEU, it doesn't compare the output with a reference answer.

items.name: Word error rate (WER)
items.summary: Share of words a speech recognizer gets wrong. Lower is better.
items.details: WER counts the substituted, deleted, and inserted words compared with a human reference transcript, divided by the number of words in the reference. It is the standard accuracy metric for speech-to-text.
items.example: A team compares WER for Amazon Transcribe with and without a custom language model on recorded support calls.
items.tip: Transcription quality → WER. Translation → BLEU. Summaries → ROUGE.

sections.title: Evaluating RAG, agents & business alignment
sections.summary: Evaluate the whole application, not just the model.

items.name: RAG evaluation
items.summary: Retrieval: context relevance and coverage. Generation: faithfulness, correctness, completeness.
items.details: Split the metrics to locate whether failures come from retrieval or generation.
items.example: Right passages + unsupported answer = low faithfulness.
items.tip: Unsupported claims despite good retrieval → low faithfulness.

items.name: Agent evaluation
items.summary: Task completion (outcome) and tool-call accuracy (trajectory).
items.details: Final wording can look fine even when the wrong action was taken.
items.example: A booking agent is scored on whether the correct room was booked.
items.tip: Agents: measure task completion and tool-call accuracy.

items.name: Business alignment metrics
items.summary: Task completion rate, user satisfaction, productivity, and cost per interaction.
items.details: Show whether the FM application meets its business objective.
items.example: Share of expense reports completed without help-desk tickets.
items.tip: Business objective questions → completion rate, satisfaction, cost per interaction.

sections.title: Responsible AI dimensions
sections.summary: Fairness, explainability, privacy & security, safety, controllability, veracity & robustness, governance, transparency.

items.name: Fairness & bias
items.summary: Outcomes and error rates shouldn't unjustly differ across groups.
items.details: Measure with subgroup analysis; dropping protected attributes isn't enough because of proxies.
items.example: A hiring model's false rejections are compared across demographic groups.
items.tip: Compare error rates across groups — overall accuracy isn't enough.

items.name: Inclusivity
items.summary: Serve all intended users, including underrepresented and accessibility needs.
items.details: Represent every group in data, evaluation, and testing.
items.example: A voice assistant is tested with older users and people with speech impairments.
items.tip: Some users poorly served → collect representative data from them.

items.name: Robustness
items.summary: Reliable behavior when inputs vary: typos, paraphrases, noise, adversarial input.
items.details: Test with perturbed and adversarial inputs.
items.example: A bot that fails on slightly reworded questions lacks robustness.
items.tip: Breaks on typos or rewording → robustness.

items.name: Veracity
items.summary: Outputs are truthful and accurate.
items.details: Hallucinated facts are veracity failures; ground and validate outputs.
items.example: Summaries that invent statistics fail veracity.
items.tip: Invented facts or statistics → veracity.

items.name: Safety
items.summary: Avoid harmful outputs and actions; add safeguards and human escalation.
items.details: Red-team before launch; route risky cases to humans.
items.example: A safety-procedures assistant escalates high-risk questions to an expert.
items.tip: Harmful guidance risk → red teaming + human escalation + guardrails.

items.name: Controllability, privacy & governance
items.summary: Ability to monitor and steer AI behavior, protect data, and assign accountability.
items.details: These dimensions connect responsible AI to security and governance (Domain 5).
items.example: A team can pause the assistant and audit its decisions.
items.tip: Ability to monitor, steer, and stop an AI system → controllability.

sections.title: Detecting & reducing bias
sections.summary: Where bias comes from and how to find it.

items.name: Dataset characteristics
items.summary: Balanced, diverse, inclusive, curated datasets with accurate labels.
items.details: Underrepresentation leads to worse performance for some groups.
items.example: A skin-condition dataset covers all skin tones and ages.
items.tip: Balanced and diverse beats simply large.

items.name: Label quality & human audits
items.summary: Biased or inconsistent labels teach biased behavior.
items.details: Audit labels with clear guidelines and knowledgeable labelers.
items.example: Dialect posts were wrongly labeled offensive, so they're relabeled.
items.tip: Biased labels → audit and relabel first.

items.name: Subgroup analysis
items.summary: Compare metrics for each relevant group, not just the overall number.
items.details: Overall accuracy can hide large gaps between groups.
items.example: 94% overall accuracy hides frequent errors for one group.
items.tip: Hidden gaps between groups → subgroup analysis.

items.name: Proxy features
items.summary: Other features can stand in for a removed sensitive attribute.
items.details: Removing gender or age columns doesn't guarantee fairness.
items.example: Postal code acts as a proxy for ethnicity.
items.tip: Dropping a sensitive column doesn't guarantee fairness.

items.name: Choosing fairness metrics
items.summary: Demographic parity, equal opportunity, and others can disagree — choose by harm and law.
items.details: Document why the chosen metric fits the use case.
items.example: A lender picks equal opportunity and documents the reasoning.
items.tip: Metrics disagree → choose by use-case harm and law; document why.

items.name: AWS tools for bias
items.summary: SageMaker Clarify (data and model bias), Model Monitor (bias drift), Bedrock evaluations (FMs).
items.details: Guardrails filter harmful content but don't measure bias in predictions.
items.example: Clarify checks training data; Model Monitor watches for drift after launch.
items.tip: Bias in ML data or predictions → Clarify. Bias drift in production → Model Monitor.

sections.title: Transparency & explainability
sections.summary: Understanding and communicating how models behave.

items.name: Transparent vs opaque models
items.summary: Interpretable models (linear, trees) can be inspected; deep networks and LLMs are black boxes.
items.details: Open weights, documented data, and licenses increase transparency.
items.example: An agency requires open weights and training data documentation before approval.
items.tip: Must inspect weights and training data → open-weight model with documentation.

items.name: Local vs global explanations
items.summary: Local explains one prediction; global summarizes feature importance across all predictions.
items.details: SHAP values (via Clarify) provide both.
items.example: A customer is told the top factors behind their premium.
items.tip: One customer's decision → local explanation.

items.name: Interpretability vs performance
items.summary: A slightly less accurate but interpretable model can be the right choice.
items.details: Requirements (regulation, safety, trust) decide the trade-off.
items.example: A hospital picks logistic regression so clinicians can validate drivers.
items.tip: Regulation requires understanding → interpretable model, even if slightly less accurate.

items.name: Transparency vs safety
items.summary: Revealing too much detail can help attackers game a model.
items.details: Give meaningful reasons and recourse without exposing exploitable internals.
items.example: A fraud model's exact rules are not published.
items.tip: Full disclosure could help people game the model → balance transparency with safety.

items.name: Transparency documentation
items.summary: SageMaker Model Cards (your models), AWS AI Service Cards (AWS services), evaluation reports.
items.details: Documentation covers intended use, limitations, and evaluation results.
items.example: A bank keeps a Model Card for every credit model.
items.tip: Your models → Model Cards. AWS's services → AI Service Cards. AWS's audits → Artifact.

sections.title: Legal & business risks of GenAI
sections.summary: IP, bias, hallucination liability, trust, and end-user harm.

items.name: Intellectual property
items.summary: Generated content may resemble protected works; training data may carry license limits.
items.details: Review outputs and check model and data licensing.
items.example: A generated image closely resembles a copyrighted character.
items.tip: Output resembles copyrighted work → IP infringement risk.

items.name: Hallucination liability & trust
items.summary: Organizations can be held responsible for what their AI tells customers.
items.details: Ground answers, check grounding, disclose limitations, and escalate uncertain cases.
items.example: A chatbot's invented refund policy leads to a customer claim.
items.tip: The company can be accountable for its chatbot's false promises.

items.name: Biased outputs & end-user risk
items.summary: Unfair or harmful outputs can harm users and damage reputation.
items.details: Evaluate for bias and toxicity; keep humans in the loop for consequential decisions.
items.example: A screening tool rejects qualified candidates from one group.
items.tip: Consequential decisions → human oversight and bias evaluation.

sections.title: Responsible model selection & human-centered design
sections.summary: Sustainability, efficiency, and designing for the people affected.

items.name: Sustainability
items.summary: Prefer the most efficient model that meets requirements; avoid unnecessary compute.
items.details: Right-size models, avoid duplicate inference and needless retraining, use efficient hardware.
items.example: Two models meet requirements; the one needing less compute is chosen.
items.tip: Equal quality, less compute → the more sustainable choice.

items.name: User feedback mechanisms
items.summary: Let users rate, comment on, and correct AI outputs.
items.details: Feedback shows where the system fails and guides improvement.
items.example: Thumbs up/down and comments on each writing suggestion.
items.tip: Learn where outputs fail → in-product ratings and comments.

items.name: AI decision transparency & recourse
items.summary: Disclose AI use, explain decisions in plain language, and offer human review.
items.details: People affected by decisions should understand them and be able to contest them.
items.example: Declined grant applicants see reasons and can request review.
items.tip: Declined with no reason → disclose AI use, give reasons, offer human review.

sections.title: Shared responsibility for AI
sections.summary: What AWS secures versus what you secure.

items.name: Security OF vs IN the cloud
items.summary: AWS secures infrastructure and managed service hosting; you secure data, access, and configuration.
items.details: With Bedrock, you own IAM, guardrails, data protection, and application behavior.
items.example: Patching model hosts is AWS's job; restricting who can invoke models is yours.
items.tip: Using a compliant service doesn't make your application compliant automatically.

sections.title: Generative AI Security Scoping Matrix
sections.summary: Five scopes that define your security responsibilities.

items.name: Scopes 1–5
items.summary: 1 consumer app · 2 enterprise app · 3 pre-trained model · 4 fine-tuned model · 5 self-trained model.
items.details: Your responsibilities grow as you move from using apps to building and training models.
items.example: A Bedrock chatbot using RAG on company documents is Scope 3.
items.tip: RAG with proprietary data is still Scope 3; changing the weights (fine-tuning) makes it Scope 4.

items.name: Security disciplines
